title: Flush toilet
description: Carries waste away and keeps the smell out of the house. Pulling a handle opens a valve so water from a cistern rushes through the bowl and down the drain. Afterwards some water stays trapped in a bend of the pipe, a plug of liquid that sewer gas cannot get past.
draw: Cutaway side view of a toilet with a cistern above it and the drain pipe beneath curving down, up and over in an S shape; the water standing in the bowl and in the lowest bend of the S is one continuous pool, level on both sides, and a lever on the cistern lifts a valve in its base.
flag: Sir John Harington built a flushing water closet in 1596; Cumming's 1775 patent added the S-bend trap. Cumming was Scottish but worked in London.

title: Refrigerated transport
description: Lets meat, fruit and milk cross oceans without spoiling, which is why shops sell food from the other side of the world. A machine on board squeezes air, cools it with seawater, then lets it expand; air that expands gets very cold, and it is blown through an insulated hold kept below freezing.
draw: Cutaway of a late-1800s steamship's hold: an insulated room with thick walls, frosty carcasses of mutton hanging from hooks, and cold-air ducts along the ceiling leading from a steam-driven compressor engine in the next compartment. Show the outer hull and the sea outside so it is clearly a ship.
flag: 1880 is the Strathleven's frozen beef and mutton from Australia to London, chilled by a Bell-Coleman air machine (Glasgow). Rivals: Charles Tellier's Frigorifique (France, 1876-77), the Paraguay (1877), Swift's iced rail cars (US, 1878), and the Dunedin (NZ, 1882), which launched the trade. Overlaps Refrigerators (1858).

title: Hydroelectric power station
description: Makes electricity from falling water. A dam holds back a river, and water rushing down a pipe through the dam spins the curved blades of a turbine; the turbine's shaft turns a generator above it, where magnets sweep past coils of copper wire and push a current through them.
draw: Cutaway of a concrete dam with the deep reservoir on one side: a large pipe slopes down through the dam to a turbine at its foot, a bladed wheel turned by the water on a vertical shaft that rises to a round generator in the power house above; spent water flows out downstream at river level.
flag: 1882 is the Vulcan Street Plant, Appleton, Wisconsin, the first hydroelectric central station (driven by a water wheel). Cragside, England, lit one house by water power in 1878.

title: Dishwasher
description: Washes a load of plates without anyone scrubbing them. Dishes stand in wire racks while a pump sprays very hot, soapy water up at them from arms below; the jets push the arms round so the spray sweeps every plate. Cochrane's first machine turned a wheel of racks through jets of hot water instead.
draw: Cutaway front view of a dishwasher with its door open: plates standing upright in a wire rack, and below them a flat spray arm on a central pivot with angled nozzles, jets of water fanning upward onto the plates; the arm spins horizontally, parallel to the floor.
flag: 1886 is Cochrane's patent; her machines sold mainly to hotels and restaurants after the 1893 Chicago fair. Electric home dishwashers came in the 1920s to 1950s.

title: Electric car
description: A carriage that runs on stored electricity instead of horses or petrol, quiet and without exhaust. A bank of lead-acid batteries feeds an electric motor that turns the wheels; around 1900 electric cars outsold petrol ones in some cities. Today's carry lithium-ion cells under the floor, and their motors run as generators when braking.
draw: A tall four-wheeled open carriage of the late 1880s with large spoked wooden wheels and no horse or shafts, a driver on a padded bench steering with a tiller; a box under the seat holds rows of battery cells, connected by wires to a small electric motor driving the rear axle by a chain.
flag: Re-dated by Boris (2026-11-22) from 2008 (the lithium-ion Tesla Roadster) to 1888, Flocken's Elektrowagen; the modern battery shows as a later part.

title: Tractor
description: Pulls ploughs, harvesters and trailers, doing the work of a team of horses without fields of oats to feed them. A petrol or diesel engine turns the big rear wheels through low gears that trade speed for pulling force, and deep treads dig into the soil so the wheels grip instead of spinning.
draw: An early farm tractor seen from the side, pulling a plough through a field: engine at the front, driver's seat over the rear axle, huge rear wheels with angled cleats or chevron treads biting into the soil, and small steerable front wheels. A drawbar links the back of the tractor to the plough, whose blades turn the soil over behind.
flag: 1892 is Froelich's petrol tractor, which threshed grain that season but sold poorly; Hart-Parr (1902) was the first commercial success and the Fordson (1917) the first mass-produced. Rubber tyres (in the hint) came only in 1932.

title: Escalator
description: Carries a steady stream of people between floors. A motor drives a loop of chain linking a staircase of metal steps; each step rides on two pairs of wheels in separate tracks, so its tread stays level as it climbs and folds flat into a moving floor at top and bottom. A rubber handrail runs alongside at the same speed.
draw: Side cutaway of an escalator between two floors: a continuous loop of linked steps, treads level on the incline and flattening out at each end, wrapping round large chain sprockets at top and bottom, with the return run of upside-down steps underneath; a black handrail loops along the top of the side panel.
flag: Reno's 1896 Coney Island 'inclined elevator' was a moving ramp with cleats, not steps; the stepped escalator came from Charles Seeberger with Otis, shown in Paris in 1900.

title: Vacuum cleaner
description: Sucks dust out of carpets instead of just stirring it into the air. A motor spins a fan that throws air out of the machine, lowering the pressure inside, so outside air rushes in through the nozzle, dragging dirt with it. A cloth bag or filter lets the air out but keeps the dust.
draw: Cutaway of an upright vacuum cleaner on a carpet: an electric motor turning a fan in a housing just above the floor nozzle, the fan blowing air up into a tall cloth bag on the handle; arrows show air going from the carpet into the nozzle, and dust is caught inside the bag.
flag: Booth's 1901 machine was a horse-drawn, petrol-engined pump parked outside the house with hoses fed through the windows; the portable electric upright came from James Spangler in 1907 (sold by Hoover from 1908).

title: Air conditioning
description: Keeps buildings cool and dry in hot weather. A liquid refrigerant evaporates inside a coil indoors, soaking up heat from the air blown across it, while water from the air condenses on the cold fins; a compressor then squeezes the vapour so it gets hot and dumps that heat outdoors through a second coil.
draw: A cutaway window air conditioner set in a window frame: on the room side a fan blows air through a cold finned coil beaded with condensation; in the middle sits a round compressor; on the outdoor side a second fan pushes air through a hot finned coil. Copper tubes join the two coils and the compressor in one closed loop.
flag: Carrier's 1902 system in a Brooklyn printing plant was built to control humidity for the paper, not for comfort.

title: Geothermal power
description: Makes electricity from the heat inside the Earth. Wells drilled deep into hot rock bring up steam, or water hot enough to flash into steam, and the steam spins a turbine that drives a generator. The cooled water is pumped back underground to be heated again.
draw: Cross-section of the ground with a layer of hot rock glowing deep below: one well pipe rises from it to a power house at the surface where steam drives a turbine and generator, white steam billows from a cooling tower beside it, and a second well pipe carries water back down into the hot rock.
flag: 1904 is Ginori Conti's test generator at Larderello lighting a few bulbs; the first geothermal power plant followed in 1911-1913.

title: Water chlorination
description: Makes tap water safe from cholera and typhoid. A small, measured dose of chlorine is mixed into the water at the treatment works, where it chemically burns through the outer walls and enzymes of bacteria and kills them. A faint trace stays in the pipes, so germs that get in later die too.
draw: A water treatment works: a dosing pipe from a tank of chlorine solution dripping steadily into the channel where water flows into a large open concrete basin of clear water, with a pipe leading on from the basin toward a distant town.
flag: Input said 1908 (Jersey City, John Leal: first continuous use in the US). First permanent chlorination was Lincoln, England, 1905 (Houston and McGowan); Middelkerke, Belgium chlorinated continuously from 1902. Chose 1905.

title: Washing machine
inventor: Alva J. Fisher, Hurley Machine Company
description: Washes a load of clothes without anyone scrubbing or wringing by hand. An electric motor turns a perforated drum, or a paddle in a tub, back and forth so soapy water is pushed through the cloth again and again; then the drum spins fast, flinging the water out through its holes.
draw: A front-loading washing machine with its round glass door shut and a cutaway side: a perforated steel drum turning on a horizontal axle, with raised ribs inside that lift the clothes and drop them into soapy water pooled at the bottom. A belt runs from an electric motor under the tub to a pulley on the back of the drum.
flag: Fisher's priority is disputed (a Binghamton firm claimed an electric washer in 1906); the Thor is usually cited as the first sold widely, from 1908.

title: Stainless steel
description: Steel that does not rust, for cutlery, sinks and surgical tools. About an eighth of it is chromium, which reacts with oxygen in the air to form a clear layer of chromium oxide only a few atoms thick. The film seals the iron off from water, and if it is scratched it forms again within moments.
draw: Two kitchen knife blades lying side by side in a shallow puddle of water: one bright, shiny and unmarked (stainless), the other an ordinary steel blade blotched with orange rust.
flag: Krupp in Germany (Benno Strauss, Eduard Maurer) patented a nickel-chromium stainless steel in 1912; Brearley's 1913 Sheffield steel is the usual credit.

title: Zipper
description: Closes a jacket, bag or tent in one pull. Each metal or plastic tooth has a bump on top and a hollow underneath; the Y-shaped slider bends the two rows apart and feeds them together at an angle, so each tooth nests between two teeth on the other side and the bumps lock into the hollows.
draw: Close-up of a metal zip half done up on a jacket, closed end at the bottom: below the slider the two rows of teeth are meshed in a single tight line; above it they spread apart in a V. The slider is a small Y-shaped channel with a wedge inside its wide top end that pushes the rows apart, and a pull tab hanging from its front.
flag: Whitcomb Judson's 'clasp locker' (1893) came first but jammed; Sundback's 1913 'Hookless No. 2' is the modern design.

title: Tower crane
description: Lifts steel and concrete to the top of tall buildings as they go up. A slim lattice mast carries a long horizontal arm that swings round; electric motors wind a steel cable over a trolley that runs out along the arm, and heavy concrete blocks on a short arm at the back balance the load.
draw: A tall tower crane against the sky: a lattice mast with an operator's cab at the top, a long horizontal jib reaching one way with a trolley and hook carrying a steel beam, and a short counter-jib the other way loaded with stacked concrete counterweight blocks.
flag: Changed from 1949: Wolff of Heilbronn showed a rail-mounted slewing tower crane at Leipzig in 1913 (company and trade sources; one says 1910). 1949 is Hans Liebherr's quick-erecting mobile tower crane, which made the type common.

title: Traffic light
description: Lets cars at a crossroads take turns instead of colliding. Coloured lamps, red for stop and green for go with amber in between, switch in a fixed cycle set by a timer or by sensors buried in the road, so each direction of traffic gets its turn.
draw: A single traffic signal on a pole at a street corner: a vertical black box with three round lamps under hooded visors, red at the top, amber in the middle, green at the bottom, with only the green lit.
flag: 1914 is Hoge's electric red-green signal in Cleveland, Ohio, switched by hand. Earlier claims: J. P. Knight's gas-lit semaphore in London (1868) and Lester Wire's electric light in Salt Lake City (1912). Input said 1912; changed to the documented Cleveland date. Automatic timers came in the 1920s.

title: Sewage treatment
description: Cleans a town's waste water before it goes back into a river. Sewage is held in tanks while air is bubbled through it, and swarms of bacteria eat the dissolved filth; the bacteria clump into a sludge that settles out, leaving clear water, and some of the sludge is fed back to start on the next batch.
draw: A long rectangular open concrete tank of brown water seen from slightly above, with air bubbles boiling up evenly across the whole surface from pipes along the bottom; beside it a round settling tank with a slowly rotating bridge arm and clear water spilling over its rim.
flag: Card describes the activated-sludge process (Ardern and Lockett, Manchester, 1914). Simpler sewage treatment (sewage farms, trickling filters) is older; 'Activated sludge' would be a more exact title.

title: Drywall
description: Lets builders put up smooth indoor walls in a day instead of plastering for a week. Wet gypsum plaster is spread between two sheets of thick paper and sets hard as its crystals regrow. Those crystals hold water locked inside them, so in a fire the board gives off steam and slows the flames.
draw: A worker holding a large pale panel against a wooden stud wall frame and driving a screw through it into a stud; the panel's cut edge faces the viewer, showing a white chalky core sandwiched between two thin layers of paper.
flag: Sackett's layered plaster-and-felt board (patent 1894) was the forerunner; US Gypsum's single-core board dates to 1916 or 1917 (sources differ).

title: Hybrid corn
inventor: George Shull, Donald Jones, Henry A. Wallace
description: Gave farmers maize that grows bigger and yields far more grain. Breeders self-pollinate corn for several generations to make pure but weak inbred lines, then cross two unrelated lines. The seed from that cross grows unusually vigorous and even, but its own seed does not, so farmers buy fresh seed every year.
draw: The edge of a seed field: a row of tall maize plants whose tassels have been pulled off their tops stands beside a row with tassels still on, shedding yellow pollen that drifts across onto the silks of the detasselled plants.
flag: Shull and East showed hybrid vigour in 1908-09 and Jones's double cross (1918) made seed affordable; Wallace's Copper Cross was first sold 1923-24 (sources differ), his seed company opened 1926, and hybrids took over the Corn Belt in the 1930s (input year 1930). Chose 1924.

title: Frozen food
description: Keeps food tasting fresh for months. Packed food is pressed between metal plates or belts chilled far below freezing, so it freezes solid in minutes rather than hours. Fast freezing forms ice crystals too small to burst the food's cells, so it is not mushy when thawed.
draw: Two long stainless-steel conveyor belts running one above the other, sandwiching a row of flat cardboard cartons of food between them; the belts are thick with frost, and icy brine sprays onto their outer faces from pipes above and below. At the far end the cartons come out frozen hard.
flag: 1924 is when Birdseye founded General Seafood to quick-freeze fish; frozen food first went on sale in shops in 1930 (Springfield, Massachusetts).

title: Prestressed concrete
description: Lets concrete beams span long gaps without cracking. Steel cables running through the beam are stretched tight and anchored at the ends, squeezing the concrete hard; concrete is strong when squeezed but weak when stretched, so when a load bends the beam, its underside only loses some of that squeeze instead of being pulled apart.
draw: Cutaway of a long concrete bridge beam with steel cables running through ducts inside it, sagging low in the middle and rising toward the ends, and a hydraulic jack at one end pulling a cable tight against a steel anchor plate on the beam's end face.
flag: 1928 is Freyssinet's patent; widespread use came after 1945.

title: Fibreglass
inventor: Games Slayter and Dale Kleist, Owens-Illinois
description: Glass spun into strands finer than a hair. A loose wool of it traps air and insulates houses; strands set in plastic resin make light, strong boats, car bodies and wind-turbine blades. Molten glass runs through hundreds of tiny holes in a hot metal plate and is pulled out into threads so thin they bend instead of snapping.
draw: Underneath a glowing-hot metal box, hundreds of fine streams of molten glass drip from rows of tiny nozzles and are drawn down into shining filaments, which converge through a guide into a single strand that winds onto a fast-spinning drum below.
flag: Kleist made glass wool by accident in 1932 and Slayter developed the process (patented 1933); the 'Fiberglas' name dates from 1936-38, and glass-fibre plastics for boats from the 1940s.

title: Polyethylene
description: The commonest plastic, used for bags, bottles, film and cable insulation. It is made by linking thousands of small molecules of ethylene gas end to end into long chains of carbon atoms; the tangled chains slide past each other when warm, so it can be moulded, but hold together as a tough, waxy solid when cool.
draw: A crinkled, translucent milky-white plastic carrier bag lying open beside a small heap of the white plastic pellets it is made from.
flag: Title changed from 'Plastics (polyethylene)': plastics as such predate it (Bakelite, 1907). 1933 is the accidental discovery at ICI Northwich; production began 1939. The hint's 'isotactic polymers' belongs to the later Ziegler-Natta catalysts (1953).

title: Blood bank
description: Keeps donated blood ready for operations and emergencies. The blood is mixed with sodium citrate, which stops it clotting by mopping up the calcium that clotting needs, and kept in a refrigerator just above freezing. Each bottle is marked with its blood type so it can go to a patient whose body won't attack it.
draw: An open hospital refrigerator with rows of glass bottles of dark red blood on wire shelves, each bottle with a plain coloured tag tied round its neck, and a little frost on the back wall.
flag: Fantus opened and named the 'blood bank' at Cook County Hospital, Chicago, in 1937; stored blood was used earlier by Oswald Robertson (1917, WWI), Sergei Yudin in Moscow (1930s) and Frederic Duran-Jorda in Barcelona (1936).

title: Heat pump
description: Heats a building with a third or less of the electricity a heater would use. It is a refrigerator run backwards: a cold refrigerant evaporates in an outdoor coil, soaking up warmth even from chilly air, ground or river water; a compressor squeezes the vapour hot, and it gives that heat up indoors as it condenses.
draw: An outdoor heat-pump unit on short feet beside a house wall: a metal box with a large round fan grille on its front and thin aluminium fins along its back, lightly frosted. Two insulated copper pipes run from its side through the wall into the house.
flag: Year changed from 1940 to 1938: the heat pump in Zurich's town hall (1937-38, drawing heat from the river Limmat) is the first large working one. Peter von Rittinger built one for an Austrian salt works in 1856; Robert Webber's home ground-source pump was about 1948 (US). Overlaps Refrigerators and Air conditioning.

title: Gas-turbine power station
description: Makes electricity from natural gas with what is essentially a jet engine bolted to the ground. A compressor squeezes air, gas burns in it, and the hot blast spins a turbine that drives a generator. Most modern plants then use the exhaust to boil water for a second, steam turbine, turning about 60 percent of the fuel's energy into electricity.
draw: Cutaway of a long horizontal gas turbine in a power hall: rows of compressor blades narrowing from the air inlet, a ring of flames in the middle, larger turbine blades after it, all on one shaft that continues into a large generator, with a duct from the hot exhaust end leading to a boiler.
flag: Re 'are these common?': yes, gas plants make about a fifth of the world's electricity and around 40% in the US, mostly combined-cycle. First gas-turbine power station: Neuchatel, Switzerland, 1939 (Brown Boveri); combined cycle from about 1960 (Korneuburg, Austria), widespread from the 1990s (the input year 1990). Chose 1939.

title: Cruise missile
description: A pilotless jet plane that flies itself to its target. A jet engine keeps it flying low on short wings while an autopilot holds the course. The first ones simply counted the distance flown with a little propeller in the nose; modern ones steer by matching radar readings of the hills below to a stored map, and by GPS.
draw: A small pilotless plane with short straight wings flying low over countryside, a long stovepipe-shaped jet engine mounted on its back above the tail with a flame at its open rear end, and a small propeller on the tip of its nose.
flag: Input year 1977 points to the modern terrain-matching type (Tomahawk, developed in the 1970s, in service 1983); the first cruise missile used in war was the German V-1 of 1944, so I used that. Change to 1983 / United States if the modern card is wanted.

title: Offshore oil platform
description: Pumps oil and gas from beneath the sea floor. A steel tower stands on legs pinned into the seabed, holding a deck above the waves with a drilling rig on top; a pipe is turned down through the water into the rock, and the oil and gas that come up are piped or shipped to shore.
draw: An offshore oil platform in open sea: a lattice of steel legs rising from the water to a flat deck carrying a tall derrick, cranes and a gas flare, with a cutaway below the waterline showing the legs reaching down to the seabed and a drill pipe going on into the rock.
flag: 1947 is Kerr-McGee's well in the Gulf of Mexico, the first out of sight of land. Earlier wells stood on piers or in shallow lakes (California 1896, Caddo Lake 1911, Lake Maracaibo 1920s).

title: Defibrillator
description: Shocks a quivering heart back into a steady beat. When the heart's muscle fibres twitch out of step it pumps no blood; a capacitor charged to a few thousand volts dumps its charge through two pads on the chest in an instant, stopping every fibre at once so the heart's natural rhythm-setter can restart them together.
draw: A portable defibrillator box open on the floor beside a person lying on their back, two flat adhesive pads stuck on the bare chest, one just below the right collarbone and one on the left side below the armpit, wires running from both pads to the box, and a kneeling rescuer's hands held clear of the body.
flag: Year changed from 1979, which is the first automated external defibrillator (the kind that reads the rhythm itself and tells a bystander when to shock). Beck first saved a patient in 1947 (Cleveland) with paddles on the bare heart during surgery; Paul Zoll shocked through the closed chest in 1956, and Bernard Lown's 1962 capacitor design is the basis of today's machines. The board already has Pacemaker (1957).

title: Randomized controlled trial
inventor: Austin Bradford Hill, Medical Research Council
description: A fair test of whether a treatment works. Patients are split into two groups purely by chance, for instance by sealed envelopes, and one group gets the treatment while the other does not. Chance spreads age, health and every hidden difference evenly, so any gap in how the groups fare is down to the treatment.
draw: On a hospital bedside table, a doctor's hand draws a card out of one of a stack of identical sealed envelopes; beside it stand two identical medicine bottles, one with a white cap and one with a blue cap, standing for the two groups. A hospital bed is softly visible behind.
flag: 1948 is the MRC streptomycin trial for tuberculosis. James Lind's 1747 scurvy test was controlled but not randomized.

title: Disposable diaper
description: A diaper you throw away instead of washing. A pad of fluffy, absorbent fibre wicks urine away from the baby's skin and holds it, and a waterproof plastic outer layer stops it leaking. Modern ones add grains of a powder that swells into a gel, holding many times its own weight of liquid.
draw: A disposable diaper cut in half and laid open to show its layers: a soft white top sheet, a thick fluffy white core of fibres flecked with tiny clear grains, and a thin shiny plastic back sheet, with a drop of water soaking into the core.
flag: Hunter Gordon's Paddi (throw-away pad in plastic pants) was patented 1948 and on sale late 1949; Marion Donovan's waterproof cover was 1949; the all-in-one disposable (Pampers, Victor Mills at Procter & Gamble) arrived in 1961.

title: Cataract lens implant
description: Restores sight to people whose own lens has clouded over with age. The surgeon removes the cloudy lens and slips a small, clear plastic one into its place behind the iris, where it bends incoming light to a sharp focus on the retina. Ridley chose the plastic of fighter-plane canopies after seeing splinters of it lie harmlessly in pilots' eyes.
draw: Cutaway side view of a human eye: a small, clear, round plastic lens with two thin curved spring arms sits just behind the iris, and light rays enter through the clear cornea and pupil, pass through the implant and converge to a point on the retina at the back.

title: Credit card
inventor: Frank McNamara and Ralph Schneider, Diners Club
description: Lets you buy now and pay later without carrying cash. The card names your account; the shop passes the charge to the card company, which pays the shop and sends you one bill a month. Later cards held the account number in a magnetic stripe, as tiny magnetised patches a reader senses, and now in a chip.
draw: A hand swiping a plain plastic card through the slot of a countertop card reader, the dark magnetic stripe on the back of the card facing into the slot where the reading head sits. No lettering or logos on the card or the reader.
flag: Diners Club (1950) was a cardboard charge card paid off monthly; BankAmericard (1958) was the first widely used revolving-credit card, and the magnetic stripe came from IBM in the 1960s.

title: Transistor hearing aid
description: Makes sounds louder for people who are hard of hearing. A tiny microphone turns sound into a weak electric current, transistors amplify it, and a small earphone turns it back into louder sound in the ear. Transistors need far less battery power than the vacuum tubes they replaced, so aids shrank to fit in a pocket, then behind the ear.
draw: A hearing aid worn behind a person's ear, partly cut away: a small curved case tucked behind the ear holds a tiny microphone, a button battery and a little circuit board, and a thin clear tube runs over the top of the ear into the ear canal.
flag: Title changed from 'Hearing aid': electric hearing aids with carbon microphones go back to Miller Reese Hutchison (1898-1902) and vacuum-tube aids to the 1920s. 1952 is the first transistor aid (Sonotone 1010, still partly tubes; all-transistor aids 1953). Alternative: keep 'Hearing aid' with year 1902.

title: Tunnel boring machine
description: Digs tunnels for railways, roads and water through solid rock. A wheel as wide as the tunnel, studded with hard steel cutters, turns while hydraulic rams press it into the rock face; rolling disc cutters crack off chips, a conveyor carries them back, and the machine braces against the walls to push itself forward.
draw: Three-quarter view inside a part-dug rock tunnel: the machine's round cutterhead fills the tunnel face, a flat steel disc studded with rows of small steel cutting wheels set in concentric rings, with slots between them for broken rock. Behind it a long trailing frame carries a conveyor belt heaped with rock back along the tunnel.
flag: Robbins's 1952 machine bored tunnels at the Oahe Dam, South Dakota; his rolling disc cutters came in 1956. Frederick Beaumont's compressed-air machine bored nearly 2 km of a trial Channel Tunnel in the early 1880s and could count as an earlier working one.

title: Centre-pivot irrigation
description: Waters a whole field with almost no labour. A long pipe carried on wheeled steel towers turns slowly round a well at the centre like the hand of a clock, spraying water from sprinklers along its length; each tower is driven forward by its own motor, so the arm sweeps out a giant green circle.
draw: A centre-pivot irrigator in a crop field seen from a low angle: a long horizontal water pipe held up by tall A-frame towers on pairs of large rubber-tyred wheels, braced by trusses underneath, with sprinklers hanging down spraying water, and the fixed central pivot tower at the far end.
flag: Zybach built a prototype around 1948 near Strasburg, Colorado; patent and first full five-tower system 1952. Early machines were driven by water pressure; electric drives came later.

title: Radiotherapy
description: Kills cancer cells with beams of radiation. In a linear accelerator, radio waves drive electrons along a tube to nearly the speed of light and smash them into a metal target to make powerful X-rays; the beam is shaped and swung round the patient from many angles, so it hits the tumour hardest and healthy tissue least.
draw: A patient lying on a treatment couch beneath a medical linear accelerator: a large C-shaped gantry whose head arches over the patient and points its beam down at the chest, the gantry able to rotate in a circle around the couch.
flag: Radiotherapy with X-rays and radium dates to 1896-1900; 1953 is the first linear-accelerator treatment (Hammersmith Hospital, London), which matches the hint. Consider retitling ('Linear accelerator radiotherapy') or redating.

title: High-voltage DC power line
description: Sends electricity hundreds of kilometres overland, or under the sea, losing less on the way than ordinary alternating current. At each end, banks of electronic switches turn AC into steady direct current and back. A steady current doesn't waste energy charging and discharging the cable's surroundings many times a second, and two wires do the work of three.
draw: A long overhead power line on tall steel pylons carrying just two thick conductor bundles, one on each side (not the three of an AC line), running from a large plain converter building toward the horizon.
flag: Title changed from the acronym. The first link (Gotland, 1954, undersea cable) used mercury-arc valves; thyristor valves, as in the hint, arrived around 1970.

title: Nuclear submarine
description: A submarine that can stay underwater for months, not hours. In its reactor, splitting uranium heats water in a sealed loop; that water boils water in a second loop into steam, which spins a turbine to drive the propeller. Because nothing burns, it needs no air, and its time submerged is limited mainly by the crew's food.
draw: Cutaway side view of a long, rounded submarine underwater: a reactor in a thick shielded compartment amidships, steam pipes running aft to a turbine, and a single shaft from the turbine to one propeller at the stern. The sail (conning tower) rises from the top of the hull ahead of the reactor.
flag: USS Nautilus was commissioned in September 1954 but first got under way on nuclear power in January 1955. Overlaps Submarine (1898) and Controlled fission reactors (1954).

title: Transistor radio
description: A radio small enough for a pocket that runs for weeks on one battery. Four transistors, tiny slivers of crystal that act as amplifiers, boost the faint signal picked up by a coil wound on a ferrite rod, doing the job of hot, power-hungry vacuum tubes, so the set needs no warm-up.
draw: A pocket-sized transistor radio with its back opened: a round speaker, a tuning dial, a small battery, a black ferrite rod wound with copper wire, and a little circuit board with a few transistors like tiny metal cans on three wire legs.
flag: Regency TR-1, October 1954.

title: Container shipping
description: Moves the world's goods cheaply in steel boxes of standard sizes. Goods are packed once at the factory, and the same sealed box rides a truck, a ship and a train without being unpacked. Cranes grab each box by locking twist-fittings into its four top corners, so a ship is unloaded in hours instead of days.
draw: A dockside gantry crane lifting a single steel shipping container off a ship stacked high with containers; the crane's rectangular lifting frame sits flat on the container's roof, locked into it at each of the four top corners, and the container hangs level beneath it on cables.

title: Disposable syringe
description: Gives injections with a needle used once and thrown away, so it cannot carry disease from one patient to the next. A rubber-tipped plunger seals against the wall of a clear plastic barrel: pulling it back lowers the pressure inside, and the outside air pressure pushes medicine up through the hollow steel needle.
draw: A clear plastic syringe with fine graduation lines (no numbers), its rubber-tipped plunger pulled halfway back, held upright beneath an upside-down glass vial; the steel needle pierces the vial's rubber stopper and liquid is rising into the barrel.
flag: First is disputed: Roehr Products (US) sold a plastic disposable syringe in 1955, Charles Rothauser (Australia) reportedly made one in 1949, Murdoch patented his in 1956, and Becton Dickinson's Plastipak (1961) made them common.

title: Intercontinental ballistic missile
description: A rocket that can carry a nuclear warhead to another continent in about half an hour. Its liquid-fuel engines burn for only a few minutes, flinging the warhead above the atmosphere to coast down a long arc like a thrown stone. Gyroscopes sense every turn, so the guidance can cut the engines at exactly the right speed and direction.
draw: A tall, slender missile standing on its launch pad, shown in cutaway: tanks of fuel and oxidiser fill most of the body, rocket engines sit at the base, and a small guidance compartment and a blunt cone-shaped warhead are at the top.
flag: First successful full-range flight: the Soviet R-7, 21 August 1957 (it also launched Sputnik). Its guidance was partly by radio from the ground, and fusion warheads on ICBMs came a year or two later.

title: Wind turbine
description: Makes electricity from the wind. Its long blades are shaped like aeroplane wings: air flowing past them creates lift that pulls each blade sideways, turning the rotor. A gearbox speeds up the slow spin to drive a generator at the top of the tower, and the whole head turns to face into the wind.
draw: A tall white tower with three long, slender blades on a hub facing into the wind; the housing at the top is cut away to show a shaft, gearbox and generator in a line. The blades are twisted along their length and wider near the hub.
flag: Distinct from Windmills by making electricity with lift-type blades. Earlier electric wind machines: James Blyth (Scotland, 1887), Charles Brush (US, 1888), Poul la Cour (Denmark, 1891). Juul's three-bladed Gedser turbine (1957) set the modern design; wind farms began around 1980 (the input year). Chose 1957.

title: Flexible endoscope
inventor: Basil Hirschowitz, Larry Curtiss, Wilbur Peters
description: Lets a doctor look inside the stomach without surgery. A bendable tube holds a bundle of thousands of glass fibres, each thinner than a hair and kept in the same order at both ends; light bounces along inside each fibre without escaping, so together they carry a picture round corners, while other fibres carry light in.
draw: A long black flexible tube curving in a loop, its tip glowing with light, with the tip cut away to show a dense bundle of hair-thin glass fibres inside; at the other end a control handle with an eyepiece for the doctor.
flag: University of Michigan; first used on a patient in 1957. Today's endoscopes mostly use a tiny camera chip at the tip instead of a fibre image bundle.

title: Spandex
description: A fibre that stretches to several times its length and springs back, used in sportswear, socks, waistbands and most stretch jeans. Its long molecules alternate soft, coiled, rubbery stretches with short stiff ones that stick to their neighbours; pulling uncoils the soft parts, and the stiff parts hold everything together so it snaps back.
draw: Two hands pulling a strip of shiny knitted stretch fabric to about twice its length, the knit loops visibly elongated in the stretched middle while the ends stay loose and gathered.
flag: Re Boris's note: a modest invention, but a few percent of it is in a large share of the world's clothing. Invented 1958; on sale (as Lycra, a brand) from about 1960-62.

title: Liquefied natural gas tanker
inventor: Constock and the British Gas Council
description: Carries natural gas across oceans where no pipeline can reach. Cooled to minus 162 °C, the gas turns to liquid and takes up only a six-hundredth of the space. It rides in heavily insulated tanks; the little that boils off carries heat away and keeps the rest cold, and the ship can burn it as fuel.
draw: A tanker ship with four large round spherical tanks rising in a row above its deck; one sphere is cut open to show a thick layer of insulation lining its wall and pale clear liquid inside giving off a wisp of vapour at the top.
flag: The Methane Pioneer, a converted wartime freighter, carried the first cargo from Lake Charles, Louisiana to Canvey Island, England in early 1959. The ship doesn't refrigerate its cargo: insulation plus boil-off keeps it cold (the hint says refrigeration).

title: Three-point seat belt
description: Holds you in your seat in a crash instead of letting you fly into the windscreen. One belt runs low across the hips and diagonally across the chest, anchored at three points, so the force lands on the strong pelvis and ribcage. A weighted catch in the reel locks the belt when the car brakes hard.
draw: A driver sitting in a car seat wearing a three-point belt: the lap part lies low across the hips, and the shoulder part runs diagonally from a mount on the door pillar above the outer shoulder, across the chest, down to a buckle beside the inner hip. The belt comes out of a reel low on the door pillar.
flag: The first 1959 Volvo belts were fixed; inertia-locking reels came a few years later.

title: Aluminium drink can
description: A light, unbreakable can for drinks that chills quickly and is easily recycled. A disc of aluminium is pressed into a shallow cup and then ironed up into a tall, thin-walled body in one piece; the domed bottom and the pressure of the drink inside keep the thin walls stiff, and a separate lid is folded onto the top.
draw: A single aluminium drink can cut in half lengthwise to show its seamless one-piece body with walls as thin as paper, the bottom domed inward, and the separate lid with its ring-pull tab crimped onto the rim.
flag: Coors's 7-ounce can, 1959; the ring-pull came in 1963 (Ermal Fraze).

title: Turbofan jet engine
description: Pushes airliners along with less fuel and less noise than a plain jet. A big fan at the front, driven by a turbine at the back, blows most of its air around the outside of the engine's core; this broad, slower stream does most of the pushing, while the core burns fuel to keep the fan turning.
draw: Cutaway side view of a turbofan engine: a large many-bladed fan at the front inside a round cowling, a narrow inner core behind it with compressor stages, a combustion chamber and turbine wheels on a shared shaft, and most of the fan's air flowing around the core through the outer duct.
flag: Rolls-Royce Conway, first turbofan in airline service (1960, Boeing 707). Its fan was small; the big high-bypass fan of the hint arrived around 1970 (GE TF39, Pratt & Whitney JT9D on the Boeing 747).

title: Planetary space probe
description: A robot spacecraft sent to fly past or orbit another planet and report back. Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity, small thrusters keep it pointed the right way, and instruments measure what it passes. A dish antenna aimed at Earth sends the readings home as a faint radio signal that giant dishes pick up.
draw: A spacecraft in space with a central boxy body, two flat rectangular solar panels spread out like wings, and a dish antenna on an arm pointed back toward a small blue Earth, while a large, cloud-covered pale yellow planet fills the other side of the frame.
flag: Mariner 2 flew past Venus on 14 December 1962, the first probe to work at another planet (Soviet Venera 1, 1961, went silent on the way). Title made singular to match the deck.

title: High-yield dwarf wheat and rice
description: Short, stiff grain plants that sharply raised harvests in Mexico and Asia in the 1960s. Fed with fertilizer, old tall varieties grew heavy heads and toppled over. Dwarfing genes from Japanese wheat and Taiwanese rice make the plant ignore part of a growth hormone's signal, so stalks stay short and upright and more of the plant goes into grain.
draw: Two wheat plants side by side in one field: a short, sturdy plant standing upright under a fat, heavy head of grain, next to a tall, thin old-style plant bent over and lying flat under its own head.
flag: Input said 1966. Borlaug's first semi-dwarf wheats (Pitic 62, Penjamo 62) were released in Mexico in 1962; the dwarf rice IR8 came from IRRI in the Philippines in 1966. Two crops on one card; could be split.

title: Hip replacement
description: Replaces a hip joint worn out by arthritis, so people can walk again without pain. A polished steel ball on a stem is fixed into the hollow of the thigh bone with bone cement and turns inside a plastic cup cemented into the pelvis. The small ball and slippery plastic keep friction and wear low for decades.
draw: Cutaway of a human hip, front view: the pelvis with a white plastic cup set into its socket, and a polished metal ball sitting in that cup, mounted on a tapered metal stem pushed down into the hollow centre of the thigh bone. The ball points up and inward toward the pelvis.
flag: Title shortened from 'Artificial hip / joint replacement'. 1962 is Charnley's switch to polyethylene cups at Wrightington Hospital; his 1958-62 Teflon cups wore out.

title: Carbon-fibre composites
inventor: William Watt, Leslie Phillips, William Johnson, Royal Aircraft Establishment
description: Makes parts stiffer and stronger than steel for their weight, for aircraft, racing bikes and tennis rackets. Threads of nearly pure carbon, each finer than a hair, are laid in the directions the load will pull and set in a hard, glue-like resin; the fibres carry the force and the resin holds them in shape.
draw: Close-up of a sheet of carbon-fibre composite with a broken edge: a glossy black resin surface showing the woven checkerboard of fibre bundles, and at the snapped edge individual hair-fine black fibres sticking out of the resin.
flag: RAE Farnborough process, 1963. Roger Bacon (Union Carbide, 1958) and Akio Shindo (Japan, 1961) made earlier strong carbon fibres.

title: Beta blockers
description: Pills that calm the heart, used for angina, high blood pressure and irregular heartbeats. Adrenaline speeds and strengthens the heartbeat by fitting into receptor molecules on heart cells called beta receptors. A beta blocker fits into the same receptors without switching them on, so adrenaline can't get in and the heart beats slower and more gently.
draw: A close-up of the surface of a heart muscle cell, drawn as a curved wall dotted with cup-shaped receptor molecules; some cups are plugged by small white drug molecules, while adrenaline molecules drift nearby unable to fit, and a faint outline of the heart is in the background.
flag: Propranolol was first used in patients in 1964 and launched as Inderal in 1965; Black's earlier pronethalol (1963) was withdrawn.

title: High-speed rail
description: Carries passengers between cities at over 200 kilometres an hour, often faster door to door than flying. Electric motors on every carriage draw power from an overhead wire through a sprung arm on the roof; the line is built with gentle curves, no level crossings and welded rails, so the train can run flat out.
draw: A streamlined bullet-nosed electric train speeding along an elevated straight track, with a spring-loaded pantograph arm on its roof pressed up against the overhead wire, which hangs from supports along the line.
flag: Tokaido Shinkansen, Tokyo to Osaka, October 1964 (210 km/h).

title: Drip irrigation
description: Waters crops a drop at a time right at the roots, using far less water than flooding or sprinklers. Plastic tubes run along each row with small drippers set into them. Inside each dripper the water squeezes through a long, narrow zigzag channel whose friction soaks up the pressure, so it seeps out slowly and evenly all along the line.
draw: Ground-level close-up of a black plastic tube lying along a row of young plants in dry soil; a small dripper in the tube releases a single drop beside one plant's stem, where a dark circle of damp soil has spread.
flag: Blass's agreement with Kibbutz Hatzerim, which founded Netafim, was signed in 1965; the first commercial drippers were sold in 1966.

title: Night vision
description: Lets soldiers, rescuers and wildlife watchers see by starlight. A lens focuses the faint light onto a coated plate where each particle of light knocks out an electron; a high voltage speeds the electrons up and multiplies them thousands of times, and they strike a phosphor screen that glows green with a bright copy of the scene.
draw: A pair of night-vision goggles mounted on the front of a helmet and flipped down: two short tubes with objective lenses facing forward and eyepieces at the back, each eyepiece glowing faint green. Dark night background.
flag: Title changed from 'Night-vision goggles': the first starlight devices (Vietnam, mid-1960s; sources give 1964-67) were rifle scopes, and head-worn goggles followed in the 1970s. Germany's 1945 'Vampir' saw by an infrared lamp rather than amplifying starlight.

title: Dental implant
description: Replaces a lost tooth with one that stays put. A small titanium screw is set into a hole drilled in the jawbone and left for some months; bone cells grow right up against the titanium and lock onto it, after which a false tooth is fixed to the top.
draw: Cross-section of a jaw showing a threaded titanium screw sunk upright into the bone between two natural teeth, the bone grown tight into its threads, a short connector post on top and a white porcelain crown fixed onto it at gum level.
flag: Brånemark, Gothenburg; first patient 1965. Earlier implant attempts did not bond with the bone.

title: Fax machine
description: Sends a copy of a page across the world over an ordinary phone line. The sending machine scans the page line by line, a light-sensitive cell turning each spot's lightness or darkness into an electrical tone; the receiving machine listens to the tones and prints matching dots, line by line, to rebuild the page.
draw: A desktop fax machine with a telephone handset resting on top, a sheet of paper being drawn face-down into its slot over a narrow bright strip of scanning light that shines across the full width of the page.
flag: Year changed from 1964 to 1966: Xerox's 1964 LDX needed special lines, while the 1966 Magnafax Telecopier (built with Magnavox) was the first to work over ordinary phone lines. Facsimile is far older: Caselli's pantelegraph ran a service in France in the 1860s, and newspapers sent wirephotos from the 1920s.

title: Mammography
description: Finds breast cancer early, often before a lump can be felt. The breast is pressed flat between two plastic plates, and low-energy X-rays pass through it onto film or a detector. Tumours and tiny specks of calcium absorb more X-rays than the soft tissue around them, so they show up as white spots.
draw: A mammography machine on its own: an upright column holding an arm with the X-ray tube head at the top, a flat detector plate at chest height below it, and a clear plastic compression paddle lowered close above the plate. No patient.
flag: Gros's Senographe (Strasbourg, 1965-66, built by CGR) was the first dedicated mammography machine; Robert Egan's film technique in Houston (1960-62) is also credited.

title: Cash machine
description: Hands out banknotes at any hour. The machine reads the customer's card, from its magnetic stripe or chip, asks for a secret number and checks both with the bank's computer over a phone line; then rollers pull notes one by one from a stack, count them and push them out through a slot.
draw: A cash machine set into a bank wall, cut away to show inside: a card slot with its reader, a keypad and screen on the front, and behind them cassettes of stacked banknotes feeding through rubber rollers up to the note slot.
flag: Title changed from 'ATM cash machine' (acronym plus repetition). First at Barclays, Enfield, 27 June 1967; it took paper vouchers marked with carbon-14, not cards. Magnetic-stripe cards and online PIN checks came in the 1970s.

title: Oral rehydration therapy
description: Saves people dying of diarrhoea with a drink of clean water, salt and sugar. Cholera makes the gut pour out water faster than a body can safely lose it. But the gut lining has carriers that pull salt and sugar in together, and water follows them by osmosis, so the drink is soaked up even while the diarrhoea goes on.
draw: A mother holding a cup to a small child's lips; on the table beside them are a jug of water, a little heap of salt, a heap of sugar and a spoon.
flag: First clinical trial at the Cholera Research Laboratory in Dhaka (then East Pakistan) in 1968; Norbert Hirschhorn (1968) and Dilip Mahalanabis (refugee camps, 1971) are also credited.

title: Precision-guided bomb
inventor: Texas Instruments and the US Air Force
description: A bomb that steers itself onto its target, landing within a few metres instead of hundreds. A laser beam lights the target with invisible pulses; a sensor in the bomb's nose sees the reflected spot and moves small fins to keep it centred as the bomb glides down. Later kinds steer by satellite navigation instead.
draw: A laser-guided bomb gliding down at a slant against the sky: a plain bomb body with a sensor head on its nose ringed by a short open collar, four small steering fins just behind the nose, and four larger fixed fins at the tail. No markings.
flag: Title made singular. Year changed from 1972 to 1968: Paveway laser-guided bombs were first used in combat in Vietnam in 1968; their famous success, dropping the Thanh Hoa bridge, was 1972. Germany's radio-guided Fritz X (1943) sank a battleship and is an earlier guided bomb.

title: Geographic information system
description: Lets planners, utilities, farmers and armies ask questions of maps by computer, such as which homes lie on flood-prone ground near a river. Each kind of information, from roads and soils to pipes and land use, is stored as its own layer pinned to the same map coordinates, so the computer can overlay them and pick out where conditions coincide.
draw: A stack of transparent map sheets floating one above another, perfectly aligned over the same patch of land: the bottom one coloured by soil type, then one with a winding river, then one with roads, then one with house outlines; a few houses on the top layer glow where they sit above the river's flood zone.
flag: Changed from 1982: Tomlinson's Canada Geographic Information System, built 1963-68 for the Canada Land Inventory, was the first working GIS (IEEE Milestone 'First GIS, 1962-1968'). 1982 is Esri's ARC/INFO, the first widely sold GIS package; restore it if the card means GIS as a commercial product.

title: Quartz watch
description: A watch accurate to a few seconds a month. A tiny quartz crystal rings thousands of times a second: squeezing quartz makes a voltage and a voltage makes it flex, so a battery-powered circuit can keep it ringing. A chip counts the vibrations and gives a little stepping motor one pulse a second to move the hands.
draw: The inside of a quartz wristwatch with the back removed: a round button battery, a small metal cylinder holding the tuning-fork-shaped quartz crystal, a microchip, and the copper coil of the stepping motor beside a train of tiny gears that turns the hands.
flag: Seiko Astron, Tokyo, December 1969; its crystal ran at 8,192 vibrations a second (modern watches use 32,768).

title: Email
description: Sends a written message to someone's computer mailbox in seconds. The message is addressed with a person's name, an @ sign and the name of their computer, and is passed from machine to machine over the network until it reaches that one. There it waits in the person's mailbox file until they log in to read it.
draw: A 1970s computer terminal: a typewriter-style keyboard with a roll of paper rising above it, a printed message shown as rows of indistinct grey lines on the paper, and a thick cable running from it to a tall cabinet of computer equipment.
flag: Tomlinson's 1971 mail between two ARPANET computers is the usual credit; messages between users of one shared computer (MIT's CTSS) date from 1965.

title: Video game console
description: Plays games on the family television. A TV draws its picture with a beam that sweeps across the screen line by line, and the console's circuits send a bright pulse at just the right moment in each sweep to put a square in a chosen spot. Turning a knob on a controller shifts that timing, so the square moves.
draw: A plain box-shaped game console on the floor wired to a 1970s wooden-cased television, with two hand controllers on cables, each with knobs on top; the screen shows two white vertical bars and a small white square ball on a black background.
flag: The first home console (1972, sold by Magnavox) was built from transistors and diodes, not microchips; single-chip consoles followed in 1975-77.

title: Artemisinin malaria drug
description: Cures malaria fast, including strains that resist older drugs. It is extracted from sweet wormwood, a herb in old Chinese fever remedies; inside the red blood cells where the parasite lives, iron from digested blood snaps a fragile oxygen bridge in the molecule, releasing reactive fragments that wreck the parasite.
draw: A leafy stem of sweet wormwood with feathery, fern-like green leaves and tiny yellow ball-shaped flowers, lying beside a glass flask of pale extract and a few white tablets.
flag: Tu Youyou's team (secret military Project 523) isolated it in 1972; Nobel Prize 2015.

title: Graphical user interface
description: Lets people use a computer by pointing at pictures instead of typing commands. Every dot on the screen is a bit in the computer's memory, so it can draw overlapping windows, icons and menus; a hand-held mouse moves an arrow across them, and clicking a picture carries out its command.
draw: A desktop computer with an upright, portrait-shaped screen showing overlapping rectangular windows, small icons and an arrow pointer (no readable text), with a keyboard in front and a three-button mouse on the desk beside it, its cable running to the computer.
flag: 1973 is the Xerox Alto, used inside Xerox. Douglas Engelbart showed windows and a mouse in 1968; the Apple Macintosh (1984) brought the idea to the public.

title: Airbag
description: A cushion that bursts out of the steering wheel in a crash and catches the head before it hits. A sensor feels the sudden slowing and fires a pellet of chemicals that turns, in about a thirtieth of a second, into nitrogen gas filling a nylon bag; vents let the bag deflate as you land on it.
draw: A car's steering wheel with a fully inflated round airbag bursting out of its centre, the torn cover flaps folded open around the hub, and the bag's fabric showing its stitched seams. Empty driver's seat behind, no person.
flag: Year changed from 1981 to 1973: GM sold airbags on some Oldsmobile Toronados in 1973 and as an option on big GM cars in 1974-76; Mercedes-Benz's 1981 S-Class is where they caught on. John Hetrick and Walter Linderer patented the idea in 1951-53.

title: Plastic drinks bottle
description: A light, shatterproof bottle that can hold fizzy drinks. A small test-tube shape of PET plastic is heated, stretched lengthwise by a rod and blown out against a mould by compressed air; the stretching lines up the plastic's long molecules in both directions, making the thin wall strong enough to hold the gas pressure.
draw: A clear plastic fizzy-drink bottle standing beside the small, thick-walled test-tube-shaped preform it was blown from, both with the same screw-thread neck, the bottle having a petal-shaped base with five feet.
flag: Title changed from 'Plastic bottle': polyethylene bottles were common by the 1950s; this card is Wyeth's stretched PET bottle for carbonated drinks (patent 1973).

title: Local area network
inventor: Robert Metcalfe and David Boggs, Xerox PARC
description: Wires the computers in an office or home together so they can share files, printers and the internet. Each machine sends data in short packets over a shared cable, listening first; if two start at the same moment, they hear the clash, both stop, and each waits a random instant before trying again. Today a switch usually gives each its own cable.
draw: An office wall with one thick cable running along it at desk height; several desktop computers sit below, each joined to it by a thin drop cable clamped on with a small box, and a bright pulse of light travels along the thick cable from one computer toward the others.
flag: Title dropped '(Ethernet)': brackets are for acronyms, and Ethernet began as a Xerox trademark. Year changed from 1983 to 1973: Metcalfe and Boggs had it running at Xerox PARC by November 1973, linking Alto computers and laser printers (the GUI card is likewise dated by internal Xerox use). First published 1976, DEC-Intel-Xerox standard 1980, first products 1981, IEEE standard 1983.

title: Pulse oximeter
description: Clips on a fingertip and shows how much oxygen the blood is carrying. Two tiny lights, one red and one infrared, shine through the finger to a light sensor on the other side. Oxygen-rich blood lets more red light through than oxygen-poor blood does, so comparing the two colours as each heartbeat swells the arteries gives the reading.
draw: Cutaway of a clip-on sensor gripping a fingertip: two tiny lights in the upper jaw (one glowing red, one infrared shown as a faint dark-red glow) shine down through the finger, past its small arteries, onto a light sensor in the lower jaw.
flag: Input said 1974. Aoyagi worked out the principle in 1972 and presented it in 1974; Nihon Kohden's first (ear) oximeter went on sale in 1975. Fingertip clips became common in the 1980s.

title: Digital camera
description: Takes photographs without film, so pictures can be seen at once and shared by computer. The lens focuses the scene onto an image-sensor chip, where light knocks electrons loose in each of millions of tiny squares; the camera measures the charge in each square and stores the numbers on a memory card.
draw: A compact digital camera cut away from the side: a lens barrel at the front, a flat rectangular sensor chip directly behind the lens, a circuit board behind that, a small memory card half pushed into its slot, and a screen on the back showing the scene in front of the lens.
flag: Sasson's 1975 prototype stored a 0.01-megapixel picture on cassette tape and was never sold; the first cameras people could buy came around 1988-91 (Fuji DS-1P, Dycam, Kodak DCS). Overlaps CCD image sensor (1969).

title: PET scanner
inventor: Michael Phelps, Edward Hoffman, Michel Ter-Pogossian
description: Shows which parts of the body are busiest, such as a tumour or a working patch of brain. The patient is injected with sugar carrying a radioactive tag that shoots out positrons, the antimatter twins of electrons; each meets an electron and both vanish into two gamma rays flying in opposite directions, which a ring of detectors catches.
draw: A patient lying on a bed that slides into a short doughnut-shaped scanner; a cutaway of the ring shows a circle of detector blocks, with two straight gamma-ray paths shooting out in exactly opposite directions from one point in the patient's head to opposite sides of the ring.
flag: Washington University, St Louis; Phelps and Hoffman's PETT scanners, 1973-75. 'PET' (positron emission tomography) is an abbreviation, not a brand, so title kept.

title: Monoclonal antibodies
description: Antibody medicines and tests aimed at one exact target, now used against cancers, arthritis and many other diseases. A white blood cell that makes one chosen antibody is fused with a cancer cell, giving a hybrid that divides forever; all its descendants pour out identical Y-shaped antibodies whose tips lock onto one molecule and nothing else.
draw: A Y-shaped antibody drawn as a folded protein, the tips of both arms gripping matching knobs on the surface of a cell like keys in locks; several more identical Y shapes drift nearby, all the same size and shape.
flag: 1975 is Köhler and Milstein's hybrid-cell method (MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge; Nobel 1984), the date history books give. First diagnostic kits about 1981; first approved antibody drug 1986 (OKT3, against kidney-transplant rejection). Köhler was German, Milstein Argentine-born.

title: Waterproof breathable fabric
inventor: Bob Gore, W. L. Gore & Associates
description: Keeps rain out while letting sweat escape, so a jacket stays dry inside. A thin film of stretched non-stick plastic (PTFE) is bonded inside the cloth; it is full of billions of tiny pores, far too small for a raindrop to squeeze through but much bigger than single molecules of water vapour, which drift out.
draw: Magnified cross-section of a jacket fabric: an outer woven layer with round raindrops beaded on top, a thin white membrane beneath riddled with tiny pores, and wisps of water vapour rising up through the pores from the warm body side below, while the drops stay on top.
flag: Changed from 1969: Bob Gore stretched PTFE into a porous membrane in 1969, but the first Gore-Tex fabric went on sale in 1976. Tightly woven Ventile cotton (England, 1940s) was an earlier waterproof breathable cloth.

title: Word processor
description: Lets people type, correct and rearrange writing on a screen before anything is printed. The words sit in the computer's memory as a long string of character codes; inserting or deleting a letter just shifts the rest along, and the program re-flows the lines to fit the page, so a document can be revised endlessly and printed clean.
draw: A late-1970s personal computer with a boxy monitor showing lines of glowing green text with a blinking block cursor in the middle of a line, and beside it a printer with a sheet of neatly typed paper feeding out.
flag: Year changed from 1983 and title shortened from 'Word processor software'. Shrayer's Electric Pencil (December 1976) was the first for personal computers; Wang's screen-based office word processors also arrived in 1976; WordStar (1978) was the first big seller. IBM's magnetic-tape typewriter (1964) was an earlier word processor with no screen.

title: Personal computer
description: A whole computer for one person, on a desk at home or work. At its heart a single microprocessor chip fetches instructions from memory chips and carries them out one after another, from hundreds of thousands to billions of times a second. A keyboard and mouse put information in, a screen shows the results, and a disk keeps files.
draw: A home desk computer: a monitor showing a simple picture, a keyboard and a mouse in front, and a tower case beside it with its side panel off to show the main circuit board, a square processor chip under a finned cooler, slim memory sticks in slots, and a disk drive in a bay.
flag: 1977 is when the Apple II, Commodore PET and TRS-80 went on sale ready-built; the Altair 8800 kit (1975) came first. Overlaps Computers (1930) and Microchips (1975).

title: Public-key encryption
inventor: Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir, Leonard Adleman
description: Lets strangers exchange secrets over an open line; it guards every secure website and card payment. Each person hands out a lock anyone can close but keeps the only key; the lock is made by multiplying two huge prime numbers, which is easy, while recovering the primes from their product would take computers longer than the age of the universe.
draw: A pile of identical open padlocks on a table, free for anyone to take, one of them snapped shut on a small metal box, and a single key on a chain held in its owner's hand.
flag: RSA (MIT, 1977) matches the prime-factoring hint. Diffie and Hellman published the public-key idea in 1976; Clifford Cocks at GCHQ found RSA in secret in 1973.

title: Anti-lock brakes
description: Stops a car's wheels locking and skidding in hard braking, so the car can still be steered. A toothed ring and a magnetic sensor at each wheel report how fast it turns. If one wheel slows much faster than the car, a microchip has valves release and reapply its brake many times a second, keeping the tyre just short of skidding.
draw: Close-up behind a car wheel: a brake disc gripped by its caliper, and beside the hub a toothed metal ring turning with the wheel, with a small sensor tip mounted just clear of the teeth and a wire leading away from it.
flag: 1978 is Bosch's digital system on the Mercedes S-Class, the usual 'first'; Chrysler and Bendix sold electronic four-wheel anti-lock on the 1971 Imperial, and Dunlop's mechanical Maxaret was used on aircraft from the 1950s and on the Jensen FF car in 1966.

title: Portable music player
description: Carries your music with you, played into lightweight headphones as you walk. The first ones played cassettes: a thin plastic tape coated with magnetised particles slides past a playback head, and the changing magnetism makes a tiny current that is amplified for the earphones. Later players store music as numbers in flash memory.
draw: A pocket cassette player with its lid open: the cassette inside, its tape running past a small metal playback head pressed against it, and a steel capstan with a rubber pinch roller squeezing the tape to pull it along. A pair of lightweight headphones on a thin wire plugged into the side.
flag: 1979 is Sony's Walkman. Transistor radios (1954) were portable earlier; digital flash-memory players arrived around 1998.

title: Spreadsheet
description: Does a business's sums on screen and redoes them instantly when any figure changes. The screen is a grid of cells, each holding a number, a label or a formula that refers to other cells; change one number and the computer recalculates every cell that depends on it, so people can ask 'what if?'.
draw: An early personal computer with a boxy monitor showing a grid of glowing green digits in rows and columns with one cell highlighted, and an office worker's hands typing on the keyboard in front.
flag: VisiCalc on the Apple II, 1979.

title: Relational database
description: Keeps the records of banks, airlines, hospitals and websites, letting thousands of people search and update them at once. Data sits in plain tables of rows and columns, linked by shared values such as a customer number; you state what you want in a short query language, and the software works out the fastest way to find and join the matching rows.
draw: Two grids of cells floating side by side like small spreadsheets with blank cells, one row in each highlighted, a glowing line joining the first cell of one highlighted row to the matching cell in the other; behind them, a tall server cabinet with stacked disk drives and blinking lights.
flag: Changed from 1983: Oracle sold the first SQL relational database in 1979 (Honeywell's MRDS, 1976, is a lesser-known earlier claim); 1983 is IBM's DB2, when they spread. Codd's founding paper was written at IBM San Jose in 1970; IBM's System R research prototype (1974-79) created SQL.

title: Hepatitis B vaccine
inventor: Baruch Blumberg, Irving Millman; Maurice Hilleman, Merck
description: Protects against a virus that causes liver failure and liver cancer; it was the first vaccine to prevent a cancer. It contains harmless copies of the virus's outer protein, which train the immune system to recognise the real thing; since 1986 that protein has been made by yeast cells given the virus gene, instead of purified from infected blood.
draw: A nurse's gloved hand giving a baby a vaccine injection in the thigh, with a small glass vial of cloudy white vaccine and a syringe on a tray beside them.
flag: 1981 is the US licence of the first vaccine, purified from carriers' blood plasma. The recombinant, yeast-made version the hint describes was licensed in 1986.

title: Home blood-glucose meter
description: Lets people with diabetes check their own blood sugar several times a day and adjust their insulin. A pricked finger puts a drop of blood on a strip whose pad holds an enzyme that reacts with sugar and darkens a dye; the meter shines a light on the pad and reads how much comes back, darker meaning more sugar.
draw: A hand-held meter with a small digital screen, a test strip pushed into its slot; a fingertip with a bead of blood touches the pad at the strip's free end, and a light inside the meter shines on the underside of the coloured pad.
flag: Ames's Glucometer (Elkhart, Indiana) went on sale for home use in November 1981; Ames's Dextrometer (1980) and Boehringer Mannheim's Accu-Chek (Germany) were near-simultaneous. Ames's Reflectance Meter (Anton Clemens, 1970) was for doctors' offices. Today's meters measure a tiny electric current instead of a colour. Overlaps Rapid test strip and Continuous glucose monitor.

title: Ivermectin
description: Kills parasitic worms, mites and lice; yearly doses have nearly wiped out river blindness in parts of Africa. Made from a substance a soil bacterium produces, it jams open a gate found only in the nerve and muscle cells of worms and insects, so charged chlorine atoms flood in and the parasite is paralysed.
draw: A village health worker holding out two small white tablets on an open palm to a child who stands against a tall wooden measuring pole painted in coloured bands, the band level with the child's head deciding the dose.
flag: 1981 is the veterinary launch; approved for people against river blindness in 1987, when Merck began giving it away free. Ōmura (Kitasato Institute) found the bacterium in soil near a golf course in Japan in 1974; Campbell's Merck team found its worm-killing power. Nobel 2015 for both.

title: Polyester fleece
description: A light, warm fabric that stays warm when wet and dries fast. Polyester fibres, often spun from melted-down plastic drinks bottles, are knitted into cloth whose surface is brushed up into a dense fuzz; the fuzz traps still air, which holds in body heat, and polyester soaks up almost no water.
draw: A folded fleece jacket with its zip half open, one corner turned back and shown magnified: a thin knitted base fabric with a thick pile of soft, curly fibres brushed up from both of its faces.
flag: Title changed from 'Polar fleece': Polarfleece was Malden Mills' trade name (later Polartec). The fabric was developed in 1979 in Lawrence, Massachusetts; Patagonia sold the first garments in 1981. Fleece from recycled bottles came in 1993.

title: ACE inhibitors
inventor: Miguel Ondetti and David Cushman, Squibb
description: Pills that lower blood pressure and ease the strain on a failing heart. The body makes a hormone that squeezes blood vessels narrow, and an enzyme snips it into its active form. The drug, modelled on a peptide from a Brazilian snake's venom, plugs that enzyme, so the vessels relax and blood flows at lower pressure.
draw: A cutaway of a small artery drawn twice side by side: on the left its muscular wall clenched tight around a narrow channel, on the right the same artery relaxed and wide with red blood cells flowing freely through it.
flag: Captopril, approved in the US in 1981; it was designed from a venom peptide that Sérgio Ferreira found in a Brazilian pit viper.

title: Compact disc
description: Plays music stored as numbers on a shiny disc. A spiral track of microscopic pits is pressed into the plastic, and a laser shines up onto it while a light sensor reads the flicker of the reflection at each pit's edges. Extra check numbers mixed in let the player rebuild sound hidden by a scratch or a speck of dust.
draw: Side cutaway of a compact disc spinning in a player: a tiny laser and lens beneath the disc focus a thin beam up onto its underside, with a magnified inset of the track showing rows of microscopic pits of different lengths.
flag: First players and discs went on sale in Japan in October 1982.

title: Computer-aided design
description: Lets engineers and architects draw on a computer instead of a drawing board. Each line, arc and surface is stored as exact numbers, the coordinates of its ends and the curve between them, rather than as ink, so a drawing can be zoomed, measured, changed and copied without redrawing, and sent straight to machines that cut the parts.
draw: An office desk with a 1980s personal computer: the screen shows a machine part as a clean line drawing in white on black, with thin dimension lines and arrows but no readable numbers; a hand on a mouse beside the keyboard, a crosshair cursor on the screen snapping to a corner of the part.
flag: Kept 1982 (AutoCAD on personal computers), matching the PC-and-mouse hint, but computer drafting is older: Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad (MIT, 1963), GM's DAC-1 (1964), and CAD systems sold to industry through the 1970s (Computervision; Dassault's CATIA, 1977). A case for an earlier year if the card means CAD in general.

title: Computer-generated imagery
description: Puts on screen things that were never in front of a camera, from film monsters to whole animated films. Every object is built as a mesh of tiny flat triangles; for each dot of the picture the computer works out how light from the lamps bounces off those surfaces into the camera, giving colour, shine and shadow, 24 pictures for every second of film.
draw: A teapot sitting on a chequered floor under a single lamp, its left half drawn as a bare wire mesh of small triangles and its right half smoothly rendered, glossy, with a bright highlight on its belly and a soft shadow falling on the floor away from the lamp.
flag: Collective. 1982 is Tron (MAGI, Triple-I and others) and Star Trek II's Genesis sequence (Lucasfilm), the first big feature-film uses. Earlier: flat computer images in Westworld (1973), a 3D hand and face in Futureworld (1976). First all-computer feature film: Toy Story (1995).

title: Solar farm
description: Makes electricity from sunlight on the scale of a power station, now the cheapest new power in most of the world. Fields of silicon-cell panels turn light into direct current, each particle of light knocking an electron loose; inverters turn it into alternating current for the grid, and many panels sit on motorised mounts that tilt to follow the sun.
draw: Long rows of dark blue solar panels across flat desert, each row mounted on a single horizontal beam running north-south and tilted so the panels face the low morning sun in the east; at the edge, a fenced box of electrical equipment and a line of power pylons.
flag: Changed from 2010: ARCO Solar's 1-megawatt plant at Hesperia (Lugo), California, began feeding the grid in late 1982, on two-axis sun trackers. 2010 marks no single event; the 2010s price fall is what made solar farms the main new power source (the round-4 reason). Overlaps Photovoltaic cells (1954).

title: Semiconductor laser
inventor: Robert N. Hall; Zhores Alferov; Izuo Hayashi and Morton Panish
description: A laser smaller than a grain of salt, cheap enough for every CD player and fibre-optic link. Current pushed into a thin layer of crystal, sandwiched between different crystals, makes electrons drop into holes and give off light; the sandwich traps both, and the polished ends act as mirrors, so the light bounces back and forth and builds into a narrow beam.
draw: A magnified tiny rectangular crystal chip sitting on a metal heat-sink block, built of flat stacked layers with one very thin layer in the middle; a fine gold wire is bonded to its top, and a narrow red beam leaves from the thin middle layer at one cut end face, spreading into an oval cone.
flag: Kept 1982, when mass-produced laser diodes went into CD players. Hall (General Electric) made the first in 1962, but it worked only in pulses, chilled in liquid nitrogen; Alferov (USSR) and Hayashi and Panish (Bell Labs) got one running continuously at room temperature in 1970; laser diodes carried telephone calls over fibre from 1977 (the board's Fiber optic communication card), so 1977 is also defensible. The hint's 'quantum well' design came later; CD lasers used the simpler sandwich.

title: Recombinant protein drugs
description: Human hormones and proteins made in bulk by microbes, starting with insulin for diabetes, which until then came from pig and cow pancreases. The human gene is spliced into bacteria or yeast, which read it as one of their own and make the human protein; huge fermentation tanks grow them, and the protein is filtered out and purified.
draw: A tall stainless-steel fermentation tank in a factory, cut away to show a frothy broth inside stirred by a central shaft with paddle blades, air bubbling up from a ring at the bottom, pipes and gauges on the outside.
flag: Human insulin, approved in the US in October 1982; Genentech engineered the bacteria (1978) and Lilly made the drug. Overlaps the board's Recombinant DNA (1970) and Genetic engineering (1973) cards.

title: PCR (DNA copying)
description: Makes billions of copies of a chosen piece of DNA in a few hours, enough to test or read. The sample is heated so the two DNA strands come apart, then cooled so short starter pieces stick to each end of the target. An enzyme from hot-spring bacteria builds a new partner strand on each, doubling the target every cycle.
draw: A benchtop DNA-copying machine with its lid open, showing a metal heating block with rows of small holes, each holding a tiny capped plastic tube of clear liquid.
flag: Mullis conceived PCR in 1983; the heat-proof Taq enzyme came in 1988 (before that, fresh enzyme was added every cycle).

title: Mobile phone
description: A telephone you carry, so you can call from almost anywhere. The land is divided into small cells, each with its own radio mast; the phone talks to the nearest one and is handed on to the next as you move. Cells far enough apart reuse the same frequencies, so millions of people can call at once.
draw: A hand holding a large brick-shaped handheld phone with a keypad and a stubby rubber antenna on top, raised toward the ear; behind, out of focus, a lattice-steel radio mast with flat panel antennas near its top.
