flag: Cooper made the first handheld call in 1973; the DynaTAC went on sale with the first US cell network in 1983. Japan (1979) and Scandinavia (1981) had cellular car-phone networks first.

title: Stealth aircraft
description: A warplane that radar can barely see. Its skin is made of flat, angled panels that bounce radar waves off in a few directions away from the transmitter, like a tilted mirror, instead of back to it; special coatings soak up much of the rest as heat, so even a large jet returns only a faint echo.
draw: A black jet seen from slightly below and ahead, built entirely of flat triangular and trapezoidal panels meeting at sharp angles, with sharply swept wings, a cockpit canopy of flat angled panes, and two tail fins splayed outward in a V. No rounded surfaces.
flag: 1983 is when the F-117 became operational (kept secret until 1988); its demonstrator Have Blue flew in 1977. The shaping rests on equations by Soviet physicist Pyotr Ufimtsev.

title: Insecticide-treated bed nets
description: Protects sleepers from the night-biting mosquitoes that spread malaria. A net over the bed keeps mosquitoes off, and its fibres are soaked or coated with insecticide, so mosquitoes that land on the mesh trying to get in are killed or driven away, even where the net is torn; when most homes use them, malaria falls for the whole village.
draw: A child asleep on a bed under a white mosquito net hanging from a ring above and tucked under the mattress on all sides, a few mosquitoes clinging to the outside of the mesh and one lying dead on the floor below.
flag: French researchers (ORSTOM) began permethrin-treated net trials in Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso, in 1983 and published in 1984; parallel early work in Tanzania and The Gambia. Long-lasting factory-treated nets came around 2000.

title: Internet
description: Links the world's computer networks into one. Every message is chopped into small packets, each labelled with where it is going; routers along the way pass each packet on toward its destination by whatever path is free, and the receiving computer puts them back in order and asks again for any that went missing.
draw: A single network router box with blinking lights and many cables plugged into its back, the cables fanning out to a laptop, a desktop computer and a fibre-optic cable whose cut end glows with light.
flag: 1 January 1983: ARPANET switched to Cerf and Kahn's TCP/IP, the usual birth date. Overlaps with the World Wide Web card.

title: Cyclosporine
description: Stops the body rejecting a transplanted kidney, liver or heart, and made those operations routine. It comes from a fungus found in a Norwegian soil sample. Inside the immune system's T cells it shuts down a signalling enzyme, so the cells that would attack the foreign organ never switch on; unlike older drugs it spares the bone marrow.
draw: A donor kidney resting in a steel dish of crushed ice in an operating theatre, its artery and vein cut short ready to be stitched in, with a row of soft oval drug capsules lying on the green surgical cloth beside the dish.
flag: Title changed from 'Anti-rejection drugs': the first one, azathioprine, made kidney transplants work from 1962, so a generic title would date to then. Borel found cyclosporine's effect at Sandoz in 1972; Roy Calne first gave it to transplant patients in Cambridge in 1978, and it was approved in 1983. Alternative: keep 'Anti-rejection drugs' and set the year to 1962.

title: Digital synthesizer and MIDI
inventor: John Chowning, Yamaha; Dave Smith and Ikutaro Kakehashi
description: Lets one keyboard or computer play and record a whole band of electronic instruments. A digital synthesizer builds sounds by arithmetic: in the common FM method, one fast wave wobbles the pitch of another, making rich bell- and brass-like tones. A standard cable sends notes as short numbered messages, which key and how hard, so any instrument can play any other.
draw: A slim electronic keyboard with a small digital display and rows of flat buttons, a hand pressing a chord on it, and a single cable with round plugs running from a socket on its back to a second keyboard behind it.
flag: 1983 is both the MIDI standard (Dave Smith of Sequential Circuits and Ikutaro Kakehashi of Roland) and Yamaha's DX7, the first mass-market digital synthesizer, using FM synthesis that Chowning invented at Stanford (1967-73). Two inventions in one card; could be split.

title: Neodymium magnet
inventor: Masato Sagawa, Sumitomo Special Metals; John Croat, General Motors
description: The strongest permanent magnet, small enough for earbuds and strong enough for electric-car motors and wind turbines. An alloy of neodymium, iron and boron is ground to powder, lined up in a magnetic field, pressed and baked solid, then magnetised; its crystals hold their magnetism so stubbornly that a disc the size of a coin can lift several kilograms of steel.
draw: A shiny silver, coin-sized disc magnet held between finger and thumb, a heavy steel spanner hanging from its underside by magnetism alone, with a few iron filings bristling up from the disc's edge.
flag: Sagawa (sintered, Japan) and Croat (melt-spun, Detroit) found the alloy independently and announced it together in 1983; Sumitomo began production in 1984. The magnets are nickel-plated because the alloy rusts. Overlaps the Rare-earth magnet card (samarium-cobalt).

title: Active-matrix LCD
description: The flat colour screen of laptops, televisions and phones. Each dot of the picture is a tiny window of liquid crystal between polarising filters, which twists light more or less to let it through. Printed on the glass behind each dot is its own transistor switch, which holds the voltage steady between refreshes, so a big screen stays sharp, fast and bright.
draw: A flat screen with one corner peeled apart into its layers: a white backlight at the bottom, a glass sheet with a fine grid of wires and a tiny transistor at the corner of each square cell, a thin liquid-crystal layer, and a top glass sheet with red, green and blue filter stripes.
flag: Brody (Westinghouse, US) built the first active-matrix LCD in 1972-73; Spear and LeComber (Dundee, Scotland) showed in 1979 that amorphous-silicon transistors could be laid on glass; the first product was Seiko Epson's pocket colour TV, Japan, 1984.

title: Desktop publishing
description: Lets one person with a computer lay out a newsletter, magazine or book that prints looking professionally typeset. Text and pictures are arranged on an on-screen page that matches the printed one; the page goes to a laser printer as a description of shapes, so each letter is drawn from its outline at the printer's full sharpness.
draw: A beige 1980s desktop computer with a separate square monitor showing a two-column newsletter page, its text as grey lines and one picture box; beside it a desktop laser printer feeding out the same page, the printed sheet half emerged.
flag: 1985 brought together Apple's LaserWriter printer, Adobe's PostScript page language and Aldus PageMaker; Aldus's Paul Brainerd coined the term.

title: DNA fingerprinting
description: Identifies a person, or their parents, from a speck of blood, hair or saliva. Everyone's DNA has short stretches repeated over and over, the number of repeats differing between people. The DNA is cut up and pulled through jelly by an electric current, which sorts the pieces by length into a pattern of bands unique to each person.
draw: A gloved hand pointing at a sheet of film laid on a glowing light box; the film shows several vertical lanes of dark horizontal bands like barcodes, and two neighbouring lanes have their bands at exactly the same heights.
flag: Changed from 1986: first used in a real case in 1985, an immigration dispute over a Ghanaian-British boy, published that year. 1986 is the first criminal case (the Narborough murders, clearing Richard Buckland); the first conviction, of Colin Pitchfork, was 1988. Jeffreys discovered the method in September 1984.

title: Coronary stent
description: Keeps a clogged heart artery open after it has been widened, without open-heart surgery. A tiny tube of metal mesh, crimped onto a deflated balloon, is threaded up through an artery from the wrist or groin; at the narrowing the balloon inflates, pressing the mesh into the wall, then deflates and is pulled out, leaving the mesh as permanent scaffolding.
draw: A cutaway of a heart artery with a yellowish fatty narrowing in its wall, a thin guide wire running through it, and a cylindrical metal-mesh tube on an inflated sausage-shaped balloon pressing the fatty deposit back, the mesh in full contact with the artery's inner wall.
flag: Re Boris's 'dont we have this?': the board has Balloon angioplasty (1977), and the shape-memory effect card mentions stents, but there is no stent card. Puel (Toulouse, March 1986) and Sigwart (Lausanne, 1986) placed the first, self-expanding steel-mesh stents; balloon-expanded stents (US approval 1994) and drug-coated ones (2002-03) took over. Heart stents are mostly balloon-expanded steel or cobalt-chrome, not shape-memory metal; nitinol self-expanding stents are used mainly in leg and neck arteries, so the hint's shape-memory effect is shaky here.

title: 3D printing
description: Builds a solid object straight from a computer design, one thin layer at a time. In the first machines an ultraviolet laser traces the shape of one slice on the surface of a vat of liquid plastic, which hardens where the light falls. The platform then sinks a fraction of a millimetre and the next slice is drawn on top.
draw: Cutaway of a vat of liquid resin with a flat perforated platform just below the surface, holding a half-built object; a thin violet laser beam comes down from a mirror above and traces on the resin surface, hardening a new layer on top of the object.
flag: Input said 1986. Hull made his first part in 1983, got his patent in 1986, and the first machine shipped in 1987 (sold commercially 1988). Most home printers instead squeeze melted plastic from a moving nozzle (Scott Crump, 1989).

title: Statins
description: Pills that lower blood cholesterol and cut the risk of heart attacks and strokes. The liver makes much of the body's cholesterol through a chain of chemical steps. A statin jams the enzyme that runs one early step, so the liver makes less and pulls more cholesterol out of the blood to make up the shortfall.
draw: A cutaway of an artery with a yellow fatty bulge in its wall narrowing the channel and red blood cells squeezing past, with a single small white pill in the foreground.
flag: Endo found the first statin in a mould at Sankyo in Japan in 1973; the first one approved for use was Merck's lovastatin (United States, 1987).

title: Flash memory
description: Keeps photos, music and files when the power is off, in phones, cameras and memory sticks. Each bit is a little charge of electrons trapped on an island of conductor sealed in very thin insulation above a transistor. A high voltage pushes electrons through the insulation by quantum tunnelling, and the trapped charge decides whether the transistor switches on.
draw: A memory stick with its plastic casing opened: a small green circuit board carrying a flat black memory chip, a smaller controller chip, and a metal plug connector at one end.
flag: Masuoka invented flash at Toshiba (NOR type shown 1984, NAND 1987); Intel sold the first flash chips in 1988, and Toshiba's NAND reached the market about 1989.

title: Keyhole surgery
description: Operations through cuts a centimetre long instead of opening the body, so patients go home in days rather than weeks. The belly is puffed up with carbon dioxide to make room; a thin telescope lit through glass fibres sends a camera picture to a screen, while the surgeon works with long, slender instruments through other small holes.
draw: An operating table seen from the side: a patient's draped, gently domed belly with three or four slim metal tubes entering it, a surgeon's gloved hands holding long thin instruments through two of them, and a video screen above showing a pink view of the inside.
flag: 1987 is Mouret's video-guided gallbladder removal in Lyon; Erich Mühe (Germany) removed one through a scope in 1985, and Kurt Semm did a keyhole appendectomy in 1980.

title: Antidepressants (SSRIs)
inventor: David Wong, Bryan Molloy, Ray Fuller, Eli Lilly
description: Eases depression and anxiety with fewer side effects than older pills. Nerve cells pass signals by releasing a messenger chemical, serotonin, into the narrow gap between them and then soaking it back up; the drug blocks that soaking-up pump, so serotonin lingers in the gap and keeps passing its signal.
draw: Magnified view of the junction between two nerve cells: the bulb-shaped end of one cell releasing small dots of serotonin across a narrow gap to receptors on the next cell, with the pump channels on the first cell's surface plugged by drug molecules so the dots stay in the gap.
flag: 1987 is US approval of fluoxetine (Lilly; on sale in Belgium 1986). Zimelidine (Arvid Carlsson, Astra, Sweden) was the first SSRI sold, in 1982, but was withdrawn; fluvoxamine followed in 1983. Older antidepressants date from 1957.

title: Rolling suitcase
description: Lets travellers pull their luggage instead of carrying it. Two small wheels are set into the bottom corners of an upright case, and a handle slides up out of the top on telescoping tubes; tipping the case back onto its wheels puts most of its weight over the axle, so the hand only steadies it and pulls.
draw: Side view of a traveller walking away from the viewer through an airport hall, an upright suitcase trailing behind them and leaning toward them, resting only on the two small wheels at the bottom edge of its face nearest them; the long metal handle rises out of the top of that same face to their hand.
flag: Plath, a Northwest Airlines pilot, built the two-wheeled, telescoping-handle case in 1987 and sold it to aircrews, then the public (Travelpro). Bernard Sadow patented a four-wheeled suitcase pulled flat by a strap in 1970.

title: Conjugate vaccines
inventor: John Robbins and Rachel Schneerson, US National Institutes of Health
description: Protects babies from meningitis and pneumonia caused by bacteria with a sugary coat. Young children's immune systems ignore sugars, so a vaccine of the coat alone fails them; chemically bolting the sugar onto a harmless protein brings the immune system's helper cells in, and the child makes lasting antibodies against the coat.
draw: A molecular-scale view of a single bacterium wrapped in a fuzzy layer of branching sugar chains; beside it, a vaccine particle: a compact, folded protein with several short sugar chains chemically attached to its surface like tassels.
flag: 1987: the first Hib conjugate vaccine licensed in the US (for toddlers; for infants from 1990). Porter Anderson and David Smith (Rochester) developed another version in parallel. Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine followed in 2000.

title: Rapid test strip
inventor: Unipath, Unilever (Keith May, Mick Prior, Ian Richards)
description: Gives a yes-or-no medical answer in minutes at home, as in pregnancy and Covid tests. A drop of urine or swab fluid soaks along a paper strip, picking up antibodies stuck to tiny coloured particles; if the substance being tested for is there, it links those particles to a line of other antibodies fixed across the strip, and a coloured line appears.
draw: A plastic test cassette lying flat, cut away to show the paper strip inside: a pad at one end with a drop of liquid soaking in, the wet front creeping along the strip, and two coloured lines showing in the result window.
flag: Clearblue One Step pregnancy test, Unipath (Unilever), Bedford, 1988: the first lateral-flow test on sale.

title: Medical abortion pill
description: Ends an early pregnancy with pills instead of surgery. A pregnancy needs the hormone progesterone to keep the lining of the womb in place; mifepristone fits into the cells' progesterone receptors without switching them on, so the lining breaks down. A second drug, misoprostol, taken a day or two later makes the womb contract and empty.
draw: A clinic table with a glass of water and a blister pack holding one pale yellow tablet, and beside it four smaller white tablets in a separate strip; a hand rests on the table next to them.
flag: Mifepristone (RU-486) was made at Roussel Uclaf in 1980 and approved in France in September 1988 (China approved it the same year). Pairing it with misoprostol became standard in the 1990s.

title: Proton-pump inhibitors
description: Pills that heal stomach ulcers and stop heartburn by cutting stomach acid. Cells in the stomach lining push acid out with tiny molecular pumps. The drug passes the stomach inside an acid-proof coating and is absorbed into the blood; in the acid around those cells it turns into a form that locks onto the pumps and jams them for a day.
draw: A cutaway of an acid-making cell in the stomach lining, its surface facing the stomach studded with small pump proteins pushing acid particles out, several of the pumps blocked by a small wedge-shaped drug molecule locked into them.
flag: Omeprazole, launched in Sweden in 1988 (US 1989); Ivan Östholm led the Astra Hässle programme. Earlier acid drugs (H2 blockers, 1976) blocked the signal to make acid, not the pump.

title: Fly-by-wire airliner
description: An airliner whose controls are worked by computers instead of cables and pulleys. The pilot's small side-stick sends electrical signals to computers, which also read gyroscopes and accelerometers; they then drive hydraulic rams that move the wing and tail surfaces, and refuse any command that would stall the plane or overstress it.
draw: The left side of an airliner cockpit: the captain's hand on a small joystick mounted on the side console beside the window, no control column in front of the seat, and screens across the panel ahead; sky through the windscreen.
flag: Airbus A320, in service April 1988. Concorde (flew 1969, in service 1976) had analogue fly-by-wire with a mechanical backup, and military jets had it in the 1970s; the A320 was the first airliner with digital computers and built-in flight-envelope protection. Uses the board's Accelerometer card.

title: Laser eye surgery
description: Corrects short sight so people can do without glasses. An ultraviolet laser fires short pulses at the clear front of the eye; each pulse breaks the chemical bonds in a layer of tissue far thinner than a hair, vaporising it without heating what's around it. Flattening the cornea's curve this way moves the eye's focus back onto the retina.
draw: Close-up of a patient lying back with one eye held open under a laser head pointing straight down; a thin flap of the clear front of the eye is folded back like a hinged lid, and the laser is reshaping the exposed tissue underneath.
flag: Input said 1995 (US approval). Trokel and Srinivasan (IBM) proposed the ultraviolet laser for the cornea in 1983; first treatments of human eyes 1987-88 (Seiler in Berlin, McDonald in the US; sources differ); first series on sighted patients, Berlin and London, 1989. The flap method (LASIK) is Ioannis Pallikaris, Greece, 1990, and the draw shows it.

title: Direct-to-home satellite TV
description: Brings hundreds of TV channels to any home with a clear view of the sky. A satellite 36,000 km above the equator circles once a day, so it hangs over one spot and beams down microwaves; a small dish focuses them onto a receiver head, which amplifies the faint signal and lowers its frequency so it can run down a cable to the TV.
draw: A small satellite dish fixed to the wall of a house: an oval dish facing up toward the sky at a slant, with a short arm sticking out from its lower edge holding a small receiver head that points back at the middle of the dish, and a cable running from the head down the wall.
flag: 1989 is Sky's launch on SES's Astra 1A satellite, the first mass-market small-dish service (Europe). Japan's NHK broadcast to small dishes from 1984, and big-dish home reception was common in the rural US from about 1980. Overlaps Communications satellites.

title: Lithium-ion battery
inventor: Akira Yoshino, John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham; Sony
description: The light, rechargeable battery in phones, laptops and electric cars. Charging drives lithium ions out of a layered metal-oxide crystal, through a liquid, and slips them between the layers of graphite in the other electrode; using the battery lets them drift back while electrons flow the long way round, through the device.
draw: A cylindrical battery cell cut open lengthwise: inside the steel can, long thin strips (copper foil coated black with graphite, a paper-thin separator, aluminium foil coated with grey metal oxide, another separator) wound together into a tight spiral roll, with the positive cap on top.
flag: Sony sold the first in 1991; Whittingham, Goodenough and Yoshino shared the 2019 Nobel Prize for it. Overlaps Lithium battery (1972).

title: World Wide Web
description: Turns the internet into a library anyone can browse. Pages are stored on computers called servers, each page with its own address; a browser program asks for a page, gets back text marked up with formatting and links, and clicking a link fetches another page from wherever in the world it lives.
draw: A boxy 1990s desktop computer whose screen shows a page of pictures and blocks of grey lines standing for text, a few highlighted links among them, with a hand on the mouse about to click one.
flag: Proposed 1989, first website December 1990, opened to the public August 1991. CERN straddles the Swiss-French border.

title: Digital cellular network (2G)
description: Made mobile phones cheap enough for billions of people, with clearer calls and text messages. The phone turns speech into compressed numbers and sends them in short bursts; each radio channel is shared by eight calls taking turns, each getting one time slot in eight. A small chip card in the phone, the SIM, proves who is paying.
draw: A small 1990s mobile phone lying face down with its back cover and battery taken off, showing a thumbnail-sized card with gold contacts slotted into a holder inside; a stubby antenna on top and a keypad visible at the edge.
flag: First call on the GSM network, Finland, 1 July 1991 (Radiolinja). The standard was written by a pan-European committee (CEPT, then ETSI), so credit is collective. Overlaps Mobile phone (1983).

title: Unicode text encoding
inventor: Joe Becker, Lee Collins and Mark Davis
description: Lets computers store and show text in every writing system, from English and Arabic to Chinese and emoji, without garbling it. Each character in the world's scripts gets its own number, over 150,000 so far, and every computer agrees on them; a compact scheme stores common letters in one byte and rarer ones in up to four.
draw: A smartphone screen showing a message thread whose bubbles hold short lines in several clearly different scripts, Latin, Arabic, Chinese and Devanagari, drawn as recognisable script shapes but not real words, with one small round smiley emoji.
flag: Unicode 1.0 published October 1991 (Becker at Xerox, Collins and Davis at Apple); UTF-8, the storage scheme the web uses, came from Ken Thompson and Rob Pike in 1992. Touches the Emoji card in the parallel batch.

title: Open-source operating system
description: Free software that runs most of the world's servers, supercomputers and phones, written by thousands of volunteers and companies. Its source code, the human-readable instructions, is published for anyone to read, change and share; changes are sent in over the Internet, reviewed, and merged by maintainers into the next version, which anyone can download.
draw: A plain beige 1990s desktop computer and monitor on a student's desk, the screen showing a black background filled with lines of light-grey start-up text, a stack of floppy disks beside the keyboard.
flag: Linux, announced by Torvalds, a Helsinki student, in August 1991, and combined with the GNU tools that Stallman's project had been writing in the US since 1983. Free BSD Unix versions followed in 1992-93.

title: Compressed media
description: Squeezes music and pictures to a tenth of their size or less, so they fit on small devices and travel quickly over the internet. Sound is split into narrow bands of pitch, and quiet sounds that the ear can't hear next to louder ones are thrown away. Photos are trimmed the same way, dropping fine detail the eye won't miss.
draw: A pair of over-ear headphones lying beside a small, plain rectangular pocket music player with a blank screen, the cable connecting them.
flag: Year from the MP3 audio standard, finalised 1992 (Fraunhofer, Germany); the JPEG picture standard is also 1992.

title: Motion-sensor chip (MEMS)
description: The accelerometer shrunk onto a silicon chip, cheap enough to fire airbags and turn phone screens. Etching carves a tiny weight hung on silicon springs, with comb-like fingers interleaved with fixed ones; when the chip speeds up or tilts, the weight lags, the gaps between the fingers change, and the chip senses the change in stored electric charge.
draw: A greatly magnified view inside a chip: a flat silicon plate suspended above the base on thin zigzag springs anchored at its corners, with rows of comb fingers sticking out of its sides that slot, without touching, between rows of fixed fingers; the plate is shifted slightly to one side, narrowing the gaps on that side.
flag: Title changed from 'MEMS motion sensors' to put a plain name first. Analog Devices announced its airbag accelerometer chip (ADXL50) in 1991, in volume production 1993. Silicon accelerometers were made in labs from 1979 (Stanford). Gyroscope chips, which sense turning with a vibrating mass, followed in the late 1990s.

title: Electric bicycle
description: A bicycle with a battery-powered motor that adds to the rider's push, making hills and long commutes easy for hundreds of millions of people. A sensor in the pedal crank measures how hard the rider presses and the motor adds a matching push; many, especially in China, are simply worked by a twist grip like a scooter's.
draw: Side view of a bicycle with a slim battery pack fixed along the frame's down tube and a wire running to a thick motor hub in the centre of the rear wheel; the chain, cranks and pedals are those of an ordinary bicycle.
flag: Changed from 2004: Yamaha's PAS (November 1993) was the first mass-produced pedal-assist bicycle. 2004 has no single event; China's e-bike boom (mostly throttle-driven, on lead-acid batteries) ran through the 2000s. Electric-bicycle patents go back to 1895 (Ogden Bolton, US).

title: Text messaging (SMS)
description: Sends a short typed message from one mobile phone to another, delivered even if the other phone is switched off. The message, up to 160 characters, rides on the radio channel the network already uses to set up calls; a message centre holds it and keeps trying until the phone reappears, then passes it on.
draw: A hand holding a 1990s mobile phone with a small grey screen and a numeric keypad, the thumb pressing a key, the screen showing a few lines of tiny indistinct block characters.
flag: The idea came from the European GSM digital-phone standards work (Hillebrand, Germany; Ghillebaert, France) in 1984-85. Neil Papworth sent the first text, from a computer to a phone, in England on 3 December 1992; the first phone-to-phone texts were in Finland in 1993. Overlaps 'Digital cellular network (2G)' in the parallel batch.

title: Genetically modified crops
description: Crops given a useful gene borrowed from another living thing. The gene is slipped into plant cells by a bacterium that naturally inserts DNA into plants, or shot in on tiny gold beads, and whole plants are grown from the changed cells. A common example makes a bacterial protein that poisons caterpillars, so the plant protects itself.
draw: An ear of corn with its husk partly peeled back, the kernels whole and undamaged, and a small caterpillar lying dead on the leaf beside it after taking a single bite.
flag: Input said 1996. First sold: Calgene's slow-softening tomato, 1994. Insect-resistant and weedkiller-tolerant corn, soy and cotton were planted widely from 1996; China grew virus-resistant GM tobacco from about 1992.

title: Online shopping
description: Lets people buy almost anything from home and have it delivered. A shop's website lists its goods; the customer's card number is scrambled by encryption on its way to the shop's computer, which checks it with the bank, and a warehouse then picks, packs and posts the order.
draw: A cardboard parcel just delivered on a doorstep, beside it through the open door a laptop on a hall table whose screen shows a grid of product pictures with one highlighted, and a bank card resting by the keyboard.
flag: Changed from 1995: the first secure web purchase was NetMarket's sale of a CD in August 1994 (Dan Kohn, Philadelphia). Amazon and eBay opened in 1995; Michael Aldrich's teleshopping over a phone line and TV (England, 1979) is an earlier claim. Inventor left blank as collective.

title: Matrix barcode (QR code)
description: Stores a web address, ticket or payment in a square of black and white blocks that any phone camera can read. Three large corner squares tell the reader where the code is and which way up it lies, so it reads at any angle; extra error-correcting blocks let it be read even with nearly a third of it smudged or torn.
draw: A phone held over a café table, its camera screen framing a square pattern of small black and white blocks printed on a card lying at an angle on the table; the pattern has three larger nested squares, in its top-left, top-right and bottom-left corners only.
flag: Title changed: 'QR Code' is a Denso Wave trademark (freely licensed, so widely treated as generic); Boris may prefer plain 'QR code'. Made to track car parts at Toyota factories. Overlaps Barcode scanner.

title: Online banking
description: Lets people check balances, pay bills and move money from home at any hour. The bank's website, reached over a secure web connection, asks for a password, then reads the bank's own account records for that customer, and turns each payment typed in into an instruction that the bank's computers carry out.
draw: A person at a kitchen table at night with a laptop open, its screen showing a web page with a list of account entries as grey lines and a balance figure; a paper bill and a bank card lie on the table beside it.
flag: Year changed from 1995: Stanford Federal Credit Union offered banking through a web browser from 1994 (trial with members in April); Wells Fargo followed in 1995. Home banking through a TV and phone line came earlier: Nottingham Building Society's Homelink (England, 1983) and New York banks' services (early 1980s).

title: Military drone
description: An aircraft with no one aboard that watches or strikes from far away, flown by a crew on the ground, perhaps on another continent. A camera ball under the nose sends live video up to a satellite and down to the crew, whose commands return the same way; long, thin wings let it circle for a day.
draw: A slender unmanned aircraft in flight, seen from below and to the side: a long thin body with a bulging rounded nose and no cockpit windows, a camera ball hanging under the nose, very long narrow straight wings, an inverted-V tail with its fins pointing downward, and a propeller at the very back pushing it along.
flag: Title made singular. 1995 is the Predator over Bosnia, the first flown by satellite link. Ryan 'Lightning Bug' spy drones flew thousands of missions over Vietnam from 1964, and Israeli drones were used over Lebanon in 1982.

title: Electronic stability control
description: Stops a car skidding out of a bend. Sensors compare where the driver is steering with how fast the car is really turning; if it starts to spin or plough straight on, a computer brakes one wheel, the outer front to stop a spin or the inner rear to tighten the turn, pulling the car back onto line.
draw: View from above of a car on a curving wet road, its tail starting to slide toward the outside of the bend; only the front wheel on the outside of the bend has its brake disc glowing, and a curved arrow shows the car's nose being pulled back toward the bend.
flag: Bosch and Mercedes-Benz, S-Class coupé, March 1995; Toyota launched a similar system later that year. Builds on Anti-lock brakes.

title: Home broadband
description: Gives homes an always-on internet connection tens of times faster than dialling up, over wires already there. A cable-TV line carries data in a few spare TV channels. A phone line, built for voice, is split into hundreds of narrow frequency bands above the pitch of speech, each carrying as much data as its noise allows, while calls go on underneath.
draw: A phone socket on a living-room wall with a small splitter plugged in, one lead going to a corded telephone and the other to a small modem box whose lights glow; a cable runs from the modem to an open laptop on a table.
flag: Title shortened from 'Home broadband (DSL and cable modem)'. Year changed from 1997 to 1995: cable internet came first (Jones Intercable, Alexandria, Virginia, October 1995; Rogers, Newmarket, Ontario, November 1995); the first commercial phone-line (ADSL) service was GTE's in California, November 1997. Collective: Rouzbeh Yassini (cable modems), Joseph Lechleider and John Cioffi (DSL).

title: Secure web connection (SSL/TLS)
description: Keeps passwords and card numbers secret on their way between your browser and a website, and proves the site is genuine. The site presents a certificate vouched for by a trusted authority; the browser uses public-key encryption to agree a fresh secret key with the site, then scrambles everything sent both ways with that key.
draw: A laptop screen showing a web payment form of empty boxes, with a small closed padlock symbol at the left end of the address bar at the top; a hand holds a plain payment card in front of the screen.
flag: SSL 2.0 shipped in Netscape's browser in February-March 1995 (version 1.0 was never released); renamed TLS in 1999.

title: Antiretroviral HIV therapy
description: Turns HIV infection from a death sentence into a condition people live with. The virus copies its genes into the cell's DNA with an enzyme called reverse transcriptase, then needs a second enzyme, protease, to finish new viruses; the drugs jam these enzymes. Taking three at once means the virus would need several lucky mutations together to escape.
draw: A weekly pill organiser with its lids open, each day's compartment holding the same trio of pills: one white oval tablet, one blue capsule and one small yellow round tablet.
flag: 1996 is three-drug combination therapy (with the new protease inhibitors), announced at the Vancouver AIDS conference; the first single drug, AZT, came in 1987. Credit is collective; David Ho is the name most often attached.

title: White LED lighting
description: Lights homes and streets on a fraction of a bulb's electricity and lasts for decades. A tiny chip of gallium nitride glows blue when current flows through it; a coating of yellow phosphor over the chip turns some of that blue light into yellow, and the blue and yellow together look white.
draw: Close-up cutaway of a single white LED: a tiny square chip glowing blue in a small metal cup, a blob of yellow phosphor covering it, and white light spreading out of the top, with two wire legs leading out below.
flag: Nichia's blue-chip-plus-yellow-phosphor white LED, 1996. Overlaps with any blue LED card (Nakamura, 1993).

title: Contactless card
description: Pays a fare or a bill with a tap, with no battery in the card. A coil of wire loops around the card's edge; the reader's coil makes a rapidly changing magnetic field that induces a current in it, powering the chip, which answers by switching its coil's load on and off, a flicker the reader detects.
draw: A see-through view of a plastic card held flat a few centimetres in front of a reader on a bus: a flat coil of wire looping several times around inside the card's edge, its two ends joined to a tiny chip, and a matching coil visible behind the reader's face.
flag: Changed from 1995: Seoul's bus card was trialled October-December 1995 and opened as a paid service in June 1996, the first contactless card in everyday use, built on Mikron's Mifare chip (Austria, 1994). Hong Kong's Octopus followed in 1997. Location is where it was first used.

title: Universal serial bus (USB)
description: One plug that connects keyboards, mice, drives and chargers to any computer. When a device is plugged in, the computer asks what it is; the device answers with a description of itself, and the computer loads the right software, no restart needed. Data then travels one bit after another down a pair of twisted wires, while two more wires carry power.
draw: A close-up of a flat rectangular plug being pushed into a matching socket on the side of a laptop, the plug's metal shell cut away to show four flat gold contacts on a plastic tongue inside, the two outer contacts slightly longer than the two inner ones.
flag: USB 1.0, January 1996, from Intel with Compaq, DEC, IBM, Microsoft, NEC and Nortel; it caught on from 1998. Title kept, though the real name is Universal Serial Bus.

title: Electronic voting machine
description: Counts a whole country's votes within hours, with no paper ballots to lose or misread. The voter presses numbered keys for a candidate and sees their name and photo on a small screen before confirming; each vote is stored in sealed memory, and when the polls close the machine prints a tally and its encrypted results are sent on for adding up.
draw: A small grey voting machine on a table behind a cardboard privacy screen, with a telephone-style numeric keypad, a coloured confirm key, and a small screen above showing a candidate's photo; a voter's finger presses one of the keys.
flag: Year changed from 2000 (when every Brazilian election went electronic): Brazil first used its machines in 1996, for about a third of voters. Earlier: the Video Voter in Illinois towns (1975-80) and India's trial at Parur, Kerala (1982), which a court struck down; India went fully electronic in 2004.

title: Mars rover
description: A robot car that drives across Mars studying rocks. Solar panels power it, and its six wheels ride on pivoting arms that let it climb over stones while keeping every wheel on the ground. Radio signals take minutes to reach Earth, so between commands it steers itself around obstacles using its own cameras.
draw: A small six-wheeled rover on red, rocky Martian ground with a flat solar panel on top; on each side a long arm pivots on the body, carrying one wheel at one end and a shorter pivoting arm with two wheels at the other, and one wheel is tilted up over a rock while the others stay down.
flag: Sojourner, July 1997, was the first rover on Mars; the Soviet Lunokhod 1 roved the Moon in 1970. Title made singular to match the deck.

title: Streaming video
description: Plays video over the internet as it arrives, instead of waiting for the whole file to download. The video is heavily compressed and sent as a stream of small packets; the player keeps a few seconds in hand and shows them in order while more arrive. Modern players drop to lower quality on the fly when the connection slows.
draw: A laptop on a kitchen table playing a film, the screen showing a person's face, with a thin progress bar along the bottom where a lighter shaded section runs ahead of the playback point.
flag: Input said 2005 (YouTube). Experiments from 1993-95; RealVideo (1997) was the first widely used streaming video. It became mainstream with YouTube (2005) and Netflix streaming (2007). Chose 1997.

title: Wireless network
description: Connects laptops, phones and printers to the internet without cables, across a home or office. A router and each device trade short radio bursts at a few billion waves a second. Newer versions split the data across dozens of neighbouring frequencies sent at once, which the receiving chip separates by Fourier analysis, so echoes off walls do not scramble it.
draw: A home wireless router on a wooden shelf: a flat box with three upright antennas and a row of small indicator lights, a laptop open on a table nearby, with faint concentric ripples spreading from the antennas to suggest radio waves.
flag: Title changed from 'Wi-Fi', a trademark. 1997 is the first standard (IEEE 802.11, committee chaired by Vic Hayes of NCR); NCR's WaveLAN (Netherlands, 1991) came before, and home use spread from 1999. The many-frequency method (OFDM) came with 802.11a/g (1999-2003), using a CSIRO (Australia) patent.

title: Hybrid car
description: Burns much less fuel in stop-start town driving. A petrol engine and an electric motor share the job of turning the wheels; when the car brakes, the motor runs as a generator and charges a battery instead of wasting the energy as heat, and that stored power helps the car pull away again.
draw: Cutaway of a small car showing a petrol engine and an electric motor-generator side by side under the bonnet, both coupled through one gearbox to the front wheels, with thick orange cables running back to a battery pack under the rear seat.
flag: Toyota Prius, December 1997. The Lohner-Porsche of 1900 was an earlier petrol-electric hybrid.

title: Social media
description: Lets people keep up with friends and share news, photos and opinions with anyone. Each person makes a profile and links to friends; a central website stores everyone's posts and, every time someone looks, a program assembles a fresh feed from the people they follow, picking and ordering what to show.
draw: A smartphone held in one hand, its screen showing a scrolling column of square photos, each with a small round profile picture beside it, the thumb in mid-scroll.
flag: Changed from 2004: SixDegrees (1997) is usually called the first social network site; Friendster (2002), MySpace (2003) and Facebook (2004) followed. Older online communities (bulletin boards, from 1978) could also claim it.

title: Ion thruster
description: Pushes a spacecraft for months on end using a tenth of a rocket's fuel. Powered by solar panels, it strips electrons off xenon atoms, and charged metal grids at the back fling the ions out at about 30 kilometres a second. The push is as gentle as a sheet of paper resting on your hand, but never lets up.
draw: The back of a spacecraft with large solar panels: a round thruster whose face is a slightly domed metal grid pierced with thousands of tiny holes, from which a faint glowing blue plume streams straight back into black space.
flag: Re Boris's note: thrust is tiny (Deep Space 1's was under a tenth of a newton) but it uses about ten times less propellant than a chemical rocket, so it wins on long missions. 1998 is Deep Space 1, the first probe driven mainly by one; Kaufman's design first flew on SERT 1 (1964). Ion and related Hall thrusters now drive probes like Dawn and keep thousands of communications satellites in orbit.

title: Search engine
description: Finds the few pages that answer a question among billions on the web. Programs crawl the web, copying every page and indexing every word; pages matching the question are then ranked, each scoring higher the more links point to it, especially links from pages that themselves rank high.
draw: A web of small rectangular pages joined by arrows, one page in the middle receiving arrows from many others and drawn larger and brighter than the rest, with a magnifying glass hovering over it.
flag: 1998 is Google's PageRank (Stanford), matching the link-ranking hint. Earlier search engines: Archie 1990, WebCrawler 1994, AltaVista 1995.

title: Fracking
description: Gets gas and oil out of dense shale rock that would otherwise hold on to it. A well is drilled down and then sideways along the rock layer; water with sand is pumped in at enormous pressure to split the rock into fine cracks, and the sand grains wedge the cracks open so the gas can seep out.
draw: Underground cross-section: a small drilling rig at the surface with a vertical well pipe that bends into a long horizontal pipe running inside a dark layer of shale far below, with fine cracks branching out from the horizontal section and grains of sand holding them open.
flag: Changed from 2000. Hydraulic fracturing dates from 1947 (Kansas), commercial from 1949. 1998 is Mitchell Energy's first successful slick-water frac in the Barnett Shale, Texas; pairing it with long horizontal wells followed around 2002-2003.

title: CMOS camera chip
inventor: Eric Fossum, NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory
description: The camera inside every phone, laptop and car. A grid of millions of light-sensitive spots on a silicon chip turns light into electric charge; unlike the older CCD chip, each spot has its own tiny amplifier, and the same cheap chip carries the circuits that read out and digitise the picture, so it needs little power.
draw: A bare image-sensor chip seen at an angle: a rectangular, mirror-like grid of tiny pixels shimmering in rainbow colours from their coloured filters, set on a small green circuit board with fine gold wires bonded around its edge, its tiny lens housing lifted off and lying beside it.
flag: Fossum's team at JPL invented the modern 'active-pixel' sensor in 1993; their spin-off Photobit sold its first off-the-shelf chip in 1998. VLSI Vision (Scotland) sold simpler CMOS sensors earlier in the 1990s; the first camera phone with one was Sharp's J-SH04 (Japan, 2000).

title: Continuous glucose monitor
description: Tracks blood sugar day and night for people with diabetes, without finger-prick tests. A hair-thin wire under the skin is coated with an enzyme that reacts with sugar in the body's fluid, making a tiny electric current: more sugar, more current. A small transmitter turns that into a reading every few minutes and can pass it to an insulin pump.
draw: Cutaway of the skin of a person's upper arm: a small round disc stuck on the surface, with a single hair-thin flexible wire running from it down into the fatty layer just below the skin, surrounded by cells bathed in fluid.
flag: Title narrowed: monitor and insulin pump are two devices. MiniMed's first monitor (US approval June 1999) recorded for three days for a doctor to read; real-time home monitors came 2004-06. Wearable insulin pumps date from Dean Kamen's of 1976, linked pump-and-sensor systems from 2006. Could be two cards.

title: Short-range wireless link
description: Links earbuds, keyboards, watches and speakers to a phone or computer across a room. Each device sends weak radio signals at 2.4 billion waves a second and hops between 79 channels 1,600 times a second, in a pattern both ends know, so it dodges interference from other gadgets nearby.
draw: A pair of small wireless earbuds lifted out of their open charging case on a table, with a smartphone lying beside them; no wires anywhere.
flag: 1999 is the first Bluetooth specification; Haartsen designed it at Ericsson from 1994, and the first products (headsets) came in 2000.

title: Graphics processor (GPU)
description: Draws the moving pictures of video games, and now does the heavy arithmetic of artificial intelligence. A screen has millions of dots, and working out each one's colour is the same small sum done over and over, so the chip packs hundreds or thousands of simple arithmetic units side by side, each taking a share and all working at once.
draw: A graphics card lying flat, its cooler and fan lifted away to show a large square chip in the centre ringed by smaller memory chips, with gold contact fingers along its bottom edge; the big chip's lid is cut away to reveal a dense, regular grid of thousands of tiny identical blocks.
flag: 1999 is Nvidia's GeForce 256, which Nvidia marketed as 'the first GPU' because it did 3D geometry on the chip; plug-in 3D accelerator cards (3dfx Voodoo, 1996) and workstation graphics came earlier. The thousands-of-units design came about 2006, when GPUs also became programmable for general sums. Overlaps Deep learning.

title: Emoji
description: Little pictures typed into messages, so a smile, a heart or a thumbs-up travels with the words. Each emoji is stored as a number code, just like a letter, so any phone can send it; the receiving phone looks the code up in its own font and draws its own picture, which is why the same emoji looks slightly different on different phones.
draw: A hand holding a smartphone showing a chat of message bubbles that contain small round yellow smiling faces, a red heart and a thumbs-up, with the on-screen keyboard open below showing a grid of such little pictures; no readable text.
flag: Changed from 2010: Kurita's set for NTT Docomo's mobile internet (1999) was used by millions in Japan; J-Phone put 90 emoji on one phone in 1997. 2010 is when Unicode added them, taking them worldwide; restore 2010 if that is the event wanted.

title: Robotic surgery
description: Lets a surgeon operate through a few small cuts using robot arms. Thin instruments and a 3D camera on long rods go in through the cuts, while the surgeon sits at a console watching the magnified view and working hand controls. Computers scale down every movement and filter out tremor, and tiny wrists at the instrument tips bend like a hand.
draw: An operating room: a patient under drapes with a large robot standing over them, its three or four slender arms angled down, each holding a long thin rod that enters the body through a small round port; a few steps away a surgeon sits at a console with face to a viewer and hands on the controls.
flag: 2000 is US approval of the first general surgical robot; its first operation on a patient was in Belgium in 1997, and an industrial robot guided a brain biopsy needle in 1985.

title: Ready-to-use therapeutic food
description: Lets starving children recover at home instead of in a hospital ward. It is a thick paste of peanuts, milk powder, sugar, oil, vitamins and minerals in a sealed foil packet; because it holds almost no water, germs cannot grow in it, so it keeps for two years without a fridge and a child can eat it straight from the packet.
draw: A mother holding a small child on her lap, the child squeezing and sucking thick brown paste from a torn-open foil sachet.
flag: Year changed from 2007 (WHO and UNICEF's endorsement): Briend and Lescanne (Nutriset) devised the paste in 1996-97, it was tried in hospitals in the late 1990s, and treatment at home began around 2000 (Steve Collins's Valid and Concern; Mark Manary in Malawi). The first-use date is soft.

title: Kinase-inhibitor cancer drugs
description: Pills that hold some cancers in check for years, first of all a leukaemia that used to be fatal. Some cancers are driven by one faulty enzyme, a kinase stuck 'on', that keeps telling cells to divide. The drug is a small molecule shaped to fit the pocket where that kinase takes in its fuel, plugging it so the signal stops.
draw: A folded protein drawn as a twisting ribbon with a deep cleft in one side, and a small drug molecule, shown as linked balls, sitting snugly in the cleft, filling it.
flag: Imatinib (Gleevec), US approval May 2001, for chronic myeloid leukaemia. Made at Ciba-Geigy (now Novartis, Basel) in the early 1990s and taken to patients by Brian Druker in Oregon.

title: Smart electricity meter
description: Measures a home's electricity and reports it to the power company by itself, so no one has to read the dial and prices can change by the hour. A chip samples the voltage and current thousands of times a second and multiplies them to get the power used; a modem sends the totals back over the power wires or by radio.
draw: A wall-mounted electricity meter with a small digital display and no spinning disc, its cover cut away to show a circuit board inside with a chip, a few thick wires from the house supply passing through a current-sensing ring, and a short antenna.
flag: Enel began fitting Italy's 30 million homes in 2001 (done by 2006), the first nationwide rollout, sending data over the power lines. Automatic meter reading was trialled from the 1970s (Theodore Paraskevakos).

title: Mobile broadband (3G data)
description: Brings the internet to a phone, fast enough for web pages, maps and video calls. Every phone transmits across the same wide band of radio at once, each signal mixed with its own fast code; the mast picks out each phone by matching that code, and data moves in packets only when there is something to send.
draw: A hand holding an early-2000s flip phone open, its small colour screen showing a tiny web page of coloured blocks, with a mast topped by flat panel antennas in the background and faint ripples of radio waves between them.
flag: NTT Docomo's W-CDMA service, Tokyo, 1 October 2001, usually called the first 3G network. The code-division radio idea was commercialised by Qualcomm (US) in 2G phones from 1995; South Korea's CDMA2000 1x (2000) is sometimes counted as 3G.

title: Online encyclopedia (wiki)
description: A free encyclopedia that anyone with a web browser can read and edit, with millions of articles in hundreds of languages. Every page has an edit button; each change is saved as a new version, so nothing is lost and a bad edit can be undone in one click, while volunteers watch the stream of recent changes and argue out disputes on discussion pages.
draw: A laptop screen showing an encyclopedia-style page split into two columns of the same paragraph side by side, comparing two versions: one line highlighted in pale red on the left and its replacement in pale green on the right, the text drawn as grey lines.
flag: Wikipedia, launched 15 January 2001. The wiki, a website any visitor can edit, was Ward Cunningham's idea (1995).

title: Video calling
description: Lets people talk face to face across the world, seeing each other as they speak. A small camera captures about thirty pictures a second; software squeezes them by sending mostly what changed since the last picture, breaks them into packets and sends them over the internet, where the other computer rebuilds and shows them alongside the sound.
draw: A laptop open on a kitchen table, a small camera lens in the frame above its screen; on the screen a grandmother's face, smiling and waving, while a child sitting in front of the laptop waves back.
flag: Collective. 2003 is when free internet video calls reached ordinary users (Apple's iChat AV with a webcam; Skype launched that year but added video in 2006). AT&T's Picturephone offered video calls over phone lines in 1964-70.

title: Electronic cigarette
description: Delivers nicotine in a mist instead of smoke, with nothing burning. A battery heats a small wire coil wound around a wick soaked in liquid: propylene glycol, glycerine, flavouring and nicotine. The liquid flash-boils off the hot wick, and the vapour cools in the air being sucked through into tiny droplets that the user breathes in.
draw: Cutaway of a pen-shaped device: a battery in the lower half; above it a small clear tank of liquid; a cotton wick passing through holes in the tank wall with a coil of thin wire wound around its middle; an air hole just below the coil and a channel from the coil up to the mouthpiece, with a wisp of mist rising.
flag: Hon Lik, a Beijing pharmacist, invented it in 2003 and it went on sale in China in 2004. His first design made the mist with a vibrating ultrasonic element; the heated coil soon replaced it. Herbert Gilbert patented a smokeless cigarette in 1963 that was never sold.

title: Podcasting
description: Free audio shows, made by anyone, that arrive on your phone or music player by themselves. The maker records an episode, saves it as a compressed sound file and adds it to a web feed, a running list on their website; the listener's app checks the feed every few hours and downloads anything new, ready to play offline.
draw: A home recording setup: a microphone on a desk arm with a round foam pop filter in front of it, a laptop showing a sound waveform, and a pair of headphones lying on the desk.
flag: The word was coined in February 2004; Winer added audio attachments to web feeds (RSS) in 2000-01, and Curry's 2004 program fetched episodes onto music players automatically.

title: Rotavirus vaccine
description: Drops swallowed by babies that protect them from rotavirus, the commonest cause of deadly diarrhoea in young children. The drops hold live but weakened virus, grown in the lab until it barely makes anyone ill; it multiplies a little in the baby's gut and trains the immune system to fight off the real thing.
draw: A health worker squeezing liquid drops from a small plastic tube into the open mouth of a baby held on its mother's lap.
flag: Year changed from 2006: the lasting vaccine (Rotarix, from Ward and Bernstein's Cincinnati strain, made by GSK) was first licensed in Mexico in July 2004; it reached Europe, and Merck's RotaTeq (Offit, Clark and Plotkin) the US, in 2006. An earlier vaccine, RotaShield (1998), was withdrawn in 1999 after rare bowel blockages.

title: GLP-1 drugs
inventor: John Eng; Amylin and Eli Lilly
description: Medicines that help people with diabetes control their blood sugar, and help many lose weight. They copy a gut hormone released after meals that tells the pancreas to release insulin, slows the stomach, and tells the brain you are full. The body's own hormone is broken down in minutes; the drugs are altered to last a day or a week.
draw: A pen-shaped injector with a dose dial at one end, its cap off and a very short fine needle at the tip, held against the skin of a person's belly.
flag: Year changed from 2017 to 2005: the first GLP-1 drug, exenatide (from Gila monster saliva, found by John Eng), was approved in 2005; 2017 is semaglutide (Novo Nordisk, Denmark) for diabetes and 2021 its approval for weight loss. Hormone research credited to Joel Habener, Svetlana Mojsov, Daniel Drucker and Jens Juul Holst.

title: Online maps and navigation
description: Shows any street on Earth, finds the way there and talks you through each turn. The world's maps and satellite photos are cut into square tiles at many zoom levels, so a phone fetches only the few it needs; satellite positioning places you on them, and distant computers plan the route using speed reports from millions of other phones to avoid traffic jams.
draw: A smartphone in a holder on a car dashboard, its screen showing a street map with one route drawn as a thick coloured line and an arrow marking the car's position at a junction; the same junction is visible through the windscreen ahead.
flag: February 2005 is Google Maps, built from the Rasmussen brothers' Where 2 Technologies in Sydney, with satellite photos from Keyhole (US). MapQuest gave web maps and driving directions from 1996; turn-by-turn phone navigation with live traffic came in 2009.

title: Distributed version control
description: Lets thousands of programmers work on the same code at once without overwriting each other. Every programmer keeps a full copy of the project and its whole history; each saved change is labelled with a fingerprint calculated from its contents, so copies can be compared and swapped over the Internet, and the software merges different people's edits line by line.
draw: A programmer's monitor showing a dark screen with a branching chart: a vertical line of coloured dots, side lines splitting off from it and later merging back in, each dot a saved version.
flag: Git, written by Torvalds in April 2005 for Linux, after the free licence for BitKeeper (2000) was withdrawn; Mercurial appeared the same month. Torvalds was living in the US by then; location could be Finland.

title: Cloud data centre
description: Lets people and companies rent computing power and storage over the internet instead of owning machines. Warehouse-sized buildings hold tens of thousands of computers in racks; software spreads each job and copies each file across many of them, so any one can fail unnoticed. Most of the electricity ends up as heat, which fans and chilled water carry away.
draw: A long, narrow aisle between two rows of tall black server racks, each packed with flat computers stacked like trays, rows of tiny green and blue lights, bundled cables, and perforated floor tiles in front of the racks blowing cool air up into them.
flag: Title made singular. 2006 is when Amazon Web Services began renting storage and computers; Google and others had built warehouse-scale data centres a few years earlier.

title: Machine translation
description: Translates text, signs and speech between dozens of languages in an instant, for free. The computer learns from millions of documents that exist in two languages, such as United Nations records, finding which words and phrases usually match which; given new text, it assembles the most likely translation. Since 2016 neural networks have done this a whole sentence at a time.
draw: A traveller holding a phone up in front of a street sign in a foreign script; on the phone screen the same sign appears, perfectly placed, but with different lettering in its place (all lettering indistinct and unreadable).
flag: 2006 is Google Translate's statistical system. Rule-based systems were in use earlier: SYSTRAN for the US Air Force (1970) and the European Commission (1976), and free on the web as AltaVista's Babel Fish (1997). The round-4 lists also proposed Neural machine translation (2016); this card covers both.

title: HPV vaccine
description: Prevents infection with the viruses behind most cervical cancers and several others. Yeast given one virus gene makes the virus's outer-shell protein, which assembles itself into empty shells that look just like the real virus but carry no genes. The immune system learns to recognise the shells and later blocks the real virus.
draw: A molecular-scale view of several identical round virus-like particles, each a ball made of 72 small five-lobed protein knobs and empty inside, floating next to a budding yeast cell.
flag: First approved June 2006 (Merck's Gardasil, US). The empty-shell idea came from Frazer and Zhou at the University of Queensland (1991), with parallel US work at the National Cancer Institute, Rochester and Georgetown.

title: Smartphone
description: A pocket computer that is also a telephone, camera, map and music player. A glass touchscreen senses fingers by the electric charge they draw, and inside are radios for calls, data and satellite positioning, a camera chip and a lithium-ion battery. A microscopic weight on springs inside a chip senses tilt, so the screen turns to match the phone.
draw: A plain smartphone with no logos or buttons held sideways in a hand, partly cut away to show its thin layers: the glass screen on top, a flat battery filling most of the body, and a small circuit board with chips near one end beside a camera lens.
flag: IBM's Simon (1994) is usually called the first smartphone; 2007 marks the touchscreen type with motion sensor, GPS and camera that the hint describes.

title: Mobile payments
description: Lets people without a bank account send and keep money using a basic mobile phone. Cash handed to a local shop agent becomes credit held by the phone company; the owner sends it to anyone with a short text message and a PIN, and the receiver turns it back into cash at another agent.
draw: Two people at the counter of a small roadside shop: a customer handing paper banknotes to the shopkeeper while holding up a simple keypad mobile phone with a short message on its tiny screen.
flag: Kept Boris's 'Mobile payments'; 'Mobile money' is the trade term and fits well since no smartphone is needed ('smartphone payments' would be wrong). M-Pesa, Kenya, March 2007; earlier text-message services: Smart Money (2001) and GCash (2004) in the Philippines.

title: OLED display
inventor: Ching Tang and Steven Van Slyke, Kodak
description: The screen in most smartphones and many TVs, thin enough to bend, where each dot makes its own light. Every pixel is a sandwich of thin films of carbon-based molecules between two electrodes; current pushed through makes them glow red, green or blue, and a tiny transistor behind each one sets its brightness. With no backlight, black pixels are simply off.
draw: A thin screen panel bent in a gentle curve, one corner cut away to show its layers: a plastic base, a layer of tiny transistors, a thin glowing layer between two electrode films, and a clear cover on top; the front shows tiny red, green and blue dots glowing.
flag: Tang and Van Slyke made the first efficient OLED at Kodak in 1987. 2007 marks the first OLED TV (Sony, Japan) and mass production of phone screens (Samsung, South Korea); small OLED screens were sold from 1997 (Pioneer car radio) and on a Kodak camera in 2003.

title: Direct oral anticoagulants
description: Pills that prevent dangerous blood clots and strokes without the blood tests and diet rules of the older warfarin. Clotting is a chain of enzymes, each switching on the next until threads of fibrin knit a clot. These drugs fit into one enzyme near the end of the chain, thrombin or factor Xa, and block it directly, so a fixed dose works predictably.
draw: Cutaway of a leg vein with red blood cells streaming freely along it; at one spot on the wall a few sticky platelets cling, trailing only short, loose strands of fibrin that never knit into a mesh; a small white tablet in the foreground.
flag: Dabigatran (Boehringer Ingelheim) was approved in Europe in March 2008, rivaroxaban (Bayer) in September 2008. An earlier one, ximelagatran (2004), was withdrawn for liver damage.

title: Off-grid solar lighting
inventor: Sam Goldman and Ned Tozun, d.light
description: Gives homes without electricity clean, bright light in place of smoky kerosene lamps. A small solar panel charges a lithium-ion battery during the day; at night the battery powers a white LED, which turns electricity into light so efficiently that a few hours of sunshine runs the lamp all evening, and often charges a phone too.
draw: A child doing homework at night by the light of a small plastic lantern on the table, its white LED shining down; a thin cable runs from the lantern to a small flat solar panel leaning against the wall by the window.
flag: d.light's first lanterns went on sale in 2008, in India and then Africa; the company grew out of a Stanford course (2006-07), so location could be India. Solar lanterns existed from the 1980s but cost too much until cheap white LEDs; pay-as-you-go home solar kits followed in 2011-12 (M-KOPA, Kenya).

title: Grid battery storage
description: Steadies the electricity grid and stores cheap solar and wind power for later. Thousands of lithium-ion cells fill rows of container-sized cabinets, and inverters turn their direct current into the grid's alternating current. When a power station trips and the grid's frequency starts to sag, they push out power within a fraction of a second, far faster than any spinning generator.
draw: Rows of identical white container-sized metal cabinets standing on gravel in open country, cooling fans on their sides, cables running to a small substation with transformers and power lines, a wind turbine in the distance.
flag: Year changed from 2017 (Hornsdale, South Australia, 100 MW, the first very large one): AES and A123's 12 MW lithium-ion plant at Los Andes, Chile, began work in November 2009 doing the same fast-frequency job. Lead-acid batteries did it earlier in West Berlin (from 1986-87), and battery banks backed up city DC networks from the 1890s. Keep 2017 if the card means the big-battery era.

title: Quadcopter drone
description: A small flying camera that anyone can steer. Four propellers on electric motors lift it, two spinning clockwise and two anticlockwise so the craft doesn't twirl; a computer reads tiny gyroscopes hundreds of times a second and speeds up or slows each motor to keep it level, tilt it and steer.
draw: A small quadcopter hovering, seen from slightly above: an X-shaped frame with a motor and two-bladed propeller at the tip of each of its four arms, diagonally opposite propellers turning the same way and neighbouring ones the opposite way, and a camera hanging below the central body.
flag: Parrot AR.Drone, shown January 2010, the first mass-market quadcopter. Earlier hobby quadcopters existed (Draganflyer, Canada, late 1990s); DJI's Phantom (2013) made camera drones common.

title: Cyberweapons
description: Software built to wreck a country's machinery, not just steal its secrets. The first known one, found in 2010, slipped into Iran's uranium plant on memory sticks through software flaws nobody knew of, hunted for the controllers of its centrifuges and made them spin too fast and then too slow, breaking them, while showing the operators normal readings.
draw: A long row of tall, slim silver cylinders standing upright in an industrial hall, joined by overhead pipes, with a laptop on a desk in the foreground that has a small memory stick plugged into its side.
flag: Stuxnet, discovered June 2010 and attributed to the US and Israel (never officially admitted); it was probably at work from 2007-09. Earlier computer worms (Morris, 1988) did damage by accident.

title: Biometric digital ID
inventor: Unique Identification Authority of India, Nandan Nilekani
description: Gives each person a number they can prove is theirs with a fingertip or an eye, even with no papers. At enrolment ten fingerprints, both irises and the face are recorded and checked against everyone on file, so nobody gets two numbers; later a scanner at a bank or shop sends a fingerprint to the central computers, which answer yes or no.
draw: A woman pressing her fingertip onto the small glass window of a hand-held fingerprint scanner held out across a shop counter, the scanner wired to a phone, the ridges of her fingertip visible where it presses on the glass.
flag: India's Aadhaar issued its first numbers in September 2010 and now covers over 1.3 billion people. Overlaps Facial recognition (parallel batch); biometric passports (2006) were left out of the list.

title: Ride-hailing apps
description: Summons a car to wherever you are standing with a tap on a phone. The phone sends its satellite-positioning fix to the company's computers, which track every nearby driver on a live map, pick the closest free one, set the fare from distance and demand, and charge your card when the ride ends. Most drivers are ordinary people in their own cars.
draw: A hand holding a smartphone showing a street map with a small car symbol moving along a road toward a pin, while in the background a car pulls up at the kerb of a city street at dusk.
flag: Year changed from 2012: Uber (then UberCab) opened in San Francisco in 2010 with hired black cars; 2012 is when Lyft and UberX let ordinary drivers use their own cars, and China's Didi started. Phone apps for booking taxis date from about 2008.

title: Voice assistant
description: Answers spoken questions and carries out spoken requests. A microphone records the voice, and software trained on huge amounts of recorded speech turns the sounds into words. Other programs work out what was meant, find an answer or take an action, and a speech synthesiser reads the reply aloud.
draw: A person holding a phone close to their mouth and speaking into it, the phone's screen showing only a glowing, pulsing wavy line.
flag: Siri grew out of SRI International's CALO project, launched as an app in 2010 and was built into the iPhone in 2011. The deep-learning speech recognition in the hint came around 2012-14. Title made singular.

title: Rocket interceptor system
description: Shoots down rockets fired at towns, while ignoring those headed for empty ground. A radar tracks each rocket moments after launch and a computer predicts where it will land; only if that is a populated area does it fire an interceptor missile, steered by radio updates and then its own radar to explode beside the rocket in mid-air.
draw: A ground launcher, a box of twenty tubes tilted steeply upward, with one interceptor missile just leaving a tube on a white smoke trail; high in the sky its trail curves to meet a small incoming rocket at a bright burst.
flag: Iron Dome; first interception 7 April 2011, near Ashkelon. Older missile defence (Patriot, from the 1980s) was built against larger missiles and is far too costly per shot for cheap rockets.

title: Cancer immunotherapy
description: Lets the body's own immune system destroy cancer, sometimes for good, even after it has spread. Killer white blood cells carry brakes, switch proteins that stop them attacking the body's own tissue, and many tumours press those brakes. The drugs are antibodies that cover the brake switches, so the killer cells go back to attacking the tumour.
draw: A microscope-style view of a small round white blood cell, its surface studded with receptors, pressed against a larger, lumpy tumour cell; Y-shaped antibodies sit on the receptors of the white blood cell, blocking a knob on the tumour cell from reaching them.
flag: 2011 is ipilimumab (US approval), from Allison's work on the CTLA-4 brake. PD-1 drugs, from Tasuku Honjo's work in Japan, followed in 2014 and are now used more; Allison and Honjo shared the 2018 Nobel. Older immunotherapy: Coley's toxins (1890s), BCG for bladder cancer (1990), interleukin-2 (1992). Builds on Monoclonal antibodies.

title: Prenatal DNA blood test
description: Checks an unborn baby for Down syndrome and some other conditions from a sample of the mother's blood, with no needle into the womb. Tiny fragments of the baby's DNA, shed by the placenta, float in her blood; the test reads millions of fragments and counts which chromosome each came from, so an extra copy of one shows up as a small surplus.
draw: A nurse drawing blood from the arm of a visibly pregnant woman seated in a clinic chair, dark red blood filling a small glass tube.
flag: Lo found the baby's DNA in the mother's blood in 1997 (at Oxford), and his team in Hong Kong showed the counting method in 2008; the first test went on sale in the US in October 2011 (Sequenom). Location could be United States.

title: CRISPR gene editing
description: Lets scientists change a chosen spot in the DNA of a living cell, to breed crops or treat inherited disease. A protein called Cas9 carries a short strand of RNA that matches the target; it slides along the DNA until the letters pair up, then cuts both strands. As the cell repairs the cut, the gene is disabled or rewritten.
draw: A molecular-scale view: a large rounded protein clamped around a stretch of DNA double helix; inside it the helix is unzipped, and a short single strand of guide RNA lies paired with one DNA strand, while just beside it both DNA strands are snipped through.
flag: Doudna (Berkeley) and Charpentier (then in Umeå, Sweden) showed the cut in a test tube in 2012; Feng Zhang and George Church used it in human cells in 2013. Nobel Prize 2020.

title: Deep learning
inventor: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Geoffrey Hinton
description: Lets computers recognise faces, speech and objects in photos by learning from examples rather than rules. Each example passes through many stacked layers of simple number-crunching units; whenever the answer comes out wrong, every connection is nudged slightly in the direction that would have shrunk the error, millions of times over.
draw: A photo of a cat on the left feeding into a column of glowing dots, then several more columns of dots joined by a dense mesh of fine lines, narrowing to a single bright dot on the right; the lines carrying strong signals glow brighter.
flag: AlexNet, University of Toronto, 2012, won the ImageNet image contest by a wide margin. Deep networks for speech recognition worked a year or two earlier; the training method (backpropagation) dates from the 1980s.

title: SGLT2 inhibitors
description: Pills for diabetes that also protect the heart and kidneys. The kidneys filter sugar out of the blood and then pull nearly all of it back in through tiny pumps lining their tubes. The drug blocks the main pump, so around 70 grams of surplus sugar a day leaves in the urine instead of staying in the blood.
draw: A cutaway of a single kidney tubule, a narrow tube lined with cells, with sugar molecules flowing along inside it; the pumps in the cells' inner wall are plugged by small drug molecules, so the sugar carries on down the tube.
flag: Year changed from 2013 (first US approval, canagliflozin): dapagliflozin, from Bristol-Myers Squibb and AstraZeneca, was approved in Europe in November 2012, the first anywhere. The idea goes back to phlorizin, a sugar-blocker from apple-tree bark (1835).

title: Software containers
description: Packs a program with everything it needs, so it runs the same on a laptop as on a thousand servers. The operating system walls each container off, giving it its own view of files and network and a fixed share of memory and processor, while all of them share one system underneath, so they start in a second and pack many to a machine.
draw: A rack-mounted server pulled out of its cabinet with its lid off, its circuit board covered by a neat row of small identical sealed boxes like miniature shipping containers, each a different colour, all sitting on the same board and drawing on the same shared bank of memory chips.
flag: Docker, 2013 (dotCloud, San Francisco; Hykes is French). The Linux features it uses came largely from Google (cgroups, 2007), which ran its own services in containers before that; FreeBSD jails (2000) and Solaris Zones (2004) were earlier. Overlaps Cloud data centre; the metaphor echoes Container shipping.

title: Hepatitis C cure
description: Cures a liver virus carried by tens of millions with two or three months of daily pills. The virus copies its genes with its own enzyme; the drug mimics one of the building blocks that enzyme uses, so the enzyme builds it into the new copy and copying stops dead. Paired with a second drug, it clears the virus in over 95% of people.
draw: A strand of viral genetic material, a long chain of beads, being copied by an enzyme drawn as a clamp sliding along it, the new matching chain trailing out behind; the new chain ends abruptly where one differently coloured bead has just been added.
flag: Sofosbuvir, US approval December 2013; invented by Michael Sofia at Pharmasset, which Gilead bought. Earlier interferon injections cured about half of patients, with harsh side effects.

title: Reusable rocket booster
description: Brings a rocket's first stage back to land after launch, so it can fly again and spaceflight costs less. The booster flips around and relights its engines to slow down, steering through the air with lattice fins near its top. It fires once more just before touchdown, unfolds four legs and settles upright on a pad or a floating barge.
draw: A tall, slim rocket booster coming down tail-first onto a flat barge at sea, a single bright engine flame pointing down at the deck, four landing legs spread out at its base, and four small lattice fins sticking out near its top.
flag: First orbital-class booster landing 21 December 2015; first re-flight 2017. Earlier partial reuse: Space Shuttle solid boosters (parachuted into the sea from 1981); Blue Origin landed a suborbital booster in November 2015.

title: Smartwatch
description: A wristwatch that counts steps, tracks sleep, measures the heartbeat and shows messages from the phone.
