A tiny accelerometer chip feels every step and movement; on the back, green lights shine into the wrist and a light sensor picks up the faint pulsing as blood, which soaks up green light, surges through the vessels with each heartbeat.
draw: A smartwatch on a wrist, shown in cutaway: on the underside of the watch two small green lights glow into the skin beside a dark light sensor, and beneath the skin a blood vessel swells with a pulse; the watch face on top shows a small heart shape.
flag: Title shortened from 'Smartwatch and fitness tracker' (two devices; today's smartwatch does both). Collective. 2015 is the Apple Watch, which with wrist heart-rate bands (Fitbit Charge HR, 2015) made them mass-market; Fitbit's clip-on step counter was 2009 and the Pebble smartwatch 2013.

title: Stroke clot retrieval
description: Pulls the blood clot out of a blocked brain artery during a stroke, often sparing the patient lasting disability. Guided by X-ray, a doctor threads a thin tube from the groin up into the brain and pushes a folded wire-mesh tube through the clot; the mesh springs open, the clot gets caught in it, and both are drawn back out.
draw: A cutaway of a brain artery blocked by a dark red clot; a thin catheter reaches the clot from below, and a cylindrical tube of open metal mesh has expanded inside the clot, the clot's material bulging through the mesh, as it is pulled back toward the catheter.
flag: Kept 2015: five trials that year (MR CLEAN, Netherlands, the first, published in early 2015) proved it works, and it became standard care. The first clot retriever (Merci, a corkscrew wire by Y. Pierre Gobin, UCLA) was approved in the US in 2004; mesh 'stent retrievers' came into use in Europe around 2009 and the US in 2012. Inventor left blank as collective.

title: Short-video feed
description: An endless stream of short phone videos, picked for each viewer by a learning program. Every swipe, replay and pause is recorded; the program compares it with the behaviour of millions of others to predict which clip will hold this viewer longest, shows that one next, and keeps retraining itself on what people actually watch.
draw: A hand holding a phone upright, the thumb mid-swipe upward; one full-screen video of a dancer slides off the top of the screen as the next, of a cooking pan, slides in from the bottom.
flag: Title made singular, from 'Short-video feed apps'. 2016 is Douyin (Beijing), launched abroad as TikTok in 2017; Vine (2013) had short clips but a feed of people you followed. Overlaps Social media.

title: End-to-end encrypted messaging
description: Lets people text and call so that nobody in between, not even the company running the service, can read the messages. Each phone keeps its own secret keys and uses public-key encryption to agree a shared key with the other phone; the key changes with every message, so a key stolen today cannot unlock older messages.
draw: Two smartphones lying face up some distance apart on a table, each showing a chat of message bubbles as grey lines, linked by a dotted arc of tiny jumbled coloured blocks with a small closed padlock at the middle of the arc.
flag: WhatsApp finished switching on end-to-end encryption for its billion users in April 2016, using the Signal protocol that Marlinspike and Perrin designed in 2013-14. Encrypted messaging existed before (PGP email 1991, Off-the-Record chat 2004) but took effort to use.

title: Facial recognition
description: Recognises a person from their face, to unlock a phone, check a passport or pick someone out of a crowd. A neural network trained on millions of photos turns each face into a list of numbers, a point in a space where pictures of the same person land close together; the system checks how close a new face is to stored ones.
draw: A person in a dim room holding a phone up in front of their face, a fine grid of faint red dots projected from the top edge of the phone and curving over their nose, cheeks and forehead to show the face's shape.
flag: Collective. 2017 is phone face unlock with a 3D infrared dot projector (Apple's iPhone X); learned face 'embeddings' came from Facebook (DeepFace, 2014) and Google (FaceNet, 2015). Face matching was used by police and casinos from the late 1990s, and Woody Bledsoe's experiments date from the 1960s.

title: Viral-vector vaccines
inventor: Public Health Agency of Canada; Merck
description: Vaccines that use a harmless virus to deliver one gene from a dangerous one. The carrier virus, stripped so it cannot cause disease, gets into cells near the injection and makes them build the target virus's surface protein, which the immune system learns to attack. An Ebola vaccine and some Covid-19 vaccines, given billions of times, work this way.
draw: A molecular-scale view: a 20-sided virus shell with thin fibres ending in knobs sticking out from its corners, docked on the surface of a human cell and passing a coiled strand of DNA inside, while a few spike-shaped proteins already stand out on the cell's surface nearby.
flag: Year changed from 2021: the first viral-vector vaccine approved for people in the West was the Ebola vaccine (a modified livestock virus, VSV, developed in Canada; used in Guinea's 2015 trial, approved 2019). China approved an adenovirus Ebola vaccine in 2017 but it saw little use; adenovirus Covid-19 vaccines (Oxford-AstraZeneca, Sputnik V) came in late 2020-21. Vaccinia-vector rabies baits for foxes were used from 1987. The picture shows an adenovirus, the commoner carrier, not VSV.

title: Self-driving car
description: A car that drives itself with nobody at the wheel. A spinning laser rangefinder on the roof measures the distance to everything around it millions of times a second, building a 3D picture, while cameras and radar add more. Deep-learning software picks out cars, people and lanes in that picture and plans a path, steering and braking on its own.
draw: An ordinary car seen from the front three-quarters driving along a city street with nobody in the driver's seat, a dome-shaped sensor housing on its roof and small sensors at its corners, with faint lines of laser light fanning out from the dome to nearby objects.
flag: Waymo opened fully driverless rides to the public in Phoenix in October 2020; driverless tests and early-rider trips ran 2017-19, and research cars go back to Ernst Dickmanns (Germany, 1980s) and the 2005 DARPA race. Title made singular.

title: mRNA vaccines
inventor: Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman; BioNTech, Moderna
description: Teaches the immune system to recognise a virus without meeting it. The injection carries genetic instructions for one virus protein, wrapped in tiny bubbles of fat; muscle cells read the instructions and make the protein, which the immune system learns to attack. The instructions fall apart within days, and the vaccine can be redesigned for a new virus in weeks.
draw: A molecular-scale view at the edge of a cell: a tiny sphere made of fat molecules, partly merged with the cell's outer membrane, releasing coiled single strands of mRNA inside; nearby a ribosome threads along one strand, and spike-shaped proteins stand out on the cell's surface.
flag: Karikó and Weissman (University of Pennsylvania, US) found the key chemical tweak in 2005 (Nobel 2023); the first approved vaccine was Pfizer-BioNTech's (BioNTech is German) in December 2020, with Moderna's (US) days later. Location could be Germany.

title: Low-orbit satellite internet
description: Brings fast internet to remote places with no cables. Thousands of small satellites circle only about 550 kilometres up, so signals make the trip quickly; a flat dish on the roof steers its beam electronically to whichever satellite is passing overhead, handing over to the next every few minutes, and the satellites relay the data to ground stations.
draw: A flat rectangular satellite dish on a farmhouse roof in open country, tilted toward the sky, with a line of small flat-panel satellites passing overhead against a starry dusk sky.
flag: Title changed from 'Satellite internet constellations' (plural and vague; Starlink is the brand). First 60 Starlink satellites launched May 2019; public service (beta) began October 2020, so year set to 2020. Internet via high geostationary satellites is older (1990s-2000s).

title: Large language models
description: Answers questions, writes and translates in everyday language. A huge neural network is trained on a vast library of text to predict the next word, adjusting billions of internal settings until it gets good at it; to reply, it predicts one word after another, each time feeding everything so far back in.
draw: A person typing at a laptop in a dim room, the screen showing a chat of alternating message bubbles with a long reply streaming in as unreadable grey lines, the screen's glow lighting their face.
flag: 2022 is ChatGPT's public release, when people began using them widely. The transformer design came from Google in 2017; GPT-3 in 2020.

title: AI image generation
inventor: OpenAI; LMU Munich and Stability AI
description: Makes a picture of whatever you describe in words. A neural network is trained by taking millions of captioned images, adding random speckle, and learning to remove it; to make a new picture it starts from pure speckle and cleans it away in dozens of small steps, each guided by the words, until an image appears.
draw: A row of five squares, left to right: the first is pure grey static; in the next a blurry patch of colour appears; then rough shapes; then a soft picture; the last is a crisp painting of a cat sitting on a sunny windowsill.
flag: 2022: DALL-E 2 (OpenAI, April), Midjourney (July) and the free Stable Diffusion (August, from Björn Ommer's lab at LMU Munich with Stability AI). The diffusion method dates from 2015 (Stanford) and 2020 (Berkeley). Overlaps Large language models and Deep learning.

title: FPV attack drone
description: A cheap racing drone turned into a guided bomb. The pilot wears video goggles showing the live view from a small camera in the drone's nose, as if sitting aboard, and steers it by radio straight into a tank, trench or vehicle, where an explosive charge strapped under it goes off. Each costs a few hundred dollars.
draw: A soldier crouching in a trench wearing boxy video goggles and holding a two-stick radio controller, while just above him a small four-propeller drone flies off with a cylindrical explosive charge strapped beneath its frame and a tiny camera pointing forward from its front.
flag: Ukrainian volunteers first adapted hobby racing drones for attack in spring 2022; mass use came in 2023. 'FPV' (first-person view) is a hobbyists' acronym; 'Drone bomb' or 'Kamikaze racing drone' would be plainer titles. Inventor left blank as collective. Overlaps Quadcopter drone (2010) and Military drone (1995).
